title: Equilibrium climate sensitivity without shared-evidence bias
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Constrain equilibrium warming from doubled CO₂ while correctly accounting for dependencies among historical, process, paleoclimate, and model evidence. Uncertainty bounds must survive plausible alternative aerosol histories, cloud feedbacks, and priors.
status: Quantitative uncertainty dates to the 1979 Charney assessment; IPCC AR6 narrowed the likely range to 2.5–4°C in 2021.
why: Determines the emissions and concentrations compatible with temperature targets.
key_works: Sherwood et al. (2020), [“An Assessment of Earth’s Climate Sensitivity Using Multiple Lines of Evidence”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019RG000678); Forster et al. (2021), [IPCC AR6, Chapter 7](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/).

title: Historical-to-future pattern-effect correction
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Predict how geographical patterns of ocean warming change global radiative feedback. Infer long-term sensitivity from historical observations without prescribing the uncertain future sea-surface-temperature pattern.
status: Intensive work since the 2010s demonstrates substantial historical effective-sensitivity biases in model experiments; the real-world correction remains uncertain.
why: Connects observed warming rates to future warming.
key_works: Gregory et al. (2020; online 2019), [“How accurately can the climate sensitivity to CO₂ be estimated from historical climate change?”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-019-04991-y).

title: Transferable trade-cumulus feedback constraints
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Determine trade-cumulus feedback across seasons, basins, mesoscale organizations, and warmer climates. Establish which observed cloud–circulation relationships remain valid as environmental conditions change.
status: EUREC4A observations reported in 2022 refuted strong mixing-desiccation feedback in sampled conditions and supported weak feedback; broader transfer remains open.
why: Tests an influential mechanism producing high simulated climate sensitivity.
key_works: Vogel et al. (2022), [“Strong cloud–circulation coupling explains weak trade cumulus feedback”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05364-y).

title: Tropical anvil optical-depth feedback
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Determine how warming changes tropical-anvil ice mass, particle sizes, optical depth, and life cycles. Quantify the resulting shortwave-plus-longwave feedback separately from changes in anvil area.
status: McKim and colleagues substantially constrained the area contribution in 2024 while identifying anvil albedo feedback as unresolved.
why: Resolves a cloud-feedback component affecting warming projections.
key_works: McKim, Bony and Dufresne (2024), [“Weak anvil cloud area feedback suggested by physical and observational constraints”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-024-01414-4).

title: Mixed-phase cloud amount versus phase feedback
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Establish the combined warming response of supercooled-liquid fraction, cloud coverage, and precipitation. Parameterizations must match cloud-top and interior observations without compensating cloud-amount and optical-depth errors.
status: A 2016 single-model constraint increased sensitivity; a 2025 multi-model analysis found opposing feedbacks that substantially offset. The cancellation’s robustness remains uncertain.
why: Controls polar and extratropical feedbacks and model sensitivity.
key_works: Tan, Storelvmo and Zelinka (2016), [“Observational constraints on mixed-phase clouds imply higher climate sensitivity”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad5300); Tan et al. (2025), [“Moderate climate sensitivity due to opposing mixed-phase cloud feedbacks”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-025-00948-7).

title: Aerosol-induced cloud adjustments beyond ship tracks
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Quantify aerosol effects on cloud fraction, liquid water, precipitation, and radiation after clouds fully adjust. Develop observational constraints transferable beyond short-lived, visibly selected ship tracks.
status: Open for decades; Glassmeier et al. (2021) showed that ship-track extrapolation can overestimate climatological cooling because slower adjustments matter.
why: Constrains warming unmasked as air pollution declines.
key_works: Glassmeier et al. (2021), [“Aerosol-cloud-climate cooling overestimated by ship-track data”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abd3980).

title: Preindustrial cloud-condensation-nuclei baseline
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Reconstruct seasonal and geographical preindustrial cloud-active aerosol populations, including natural sulfur, sea spray, dust, and organics. Determine how modern measurements constrain this counterfactual despite nonlinear cloud susceptibility.
status: Carslaw et al. (2013) quantified a large natural-aerosol contribution to forcing uncertainty; the preindustrial atmosphere remains indirectly reconstructed.
why: Aerosol forcing depends on the difference between industrial and preindustrial states.
key_works: Carslaw et al. (2013), [“Large contribution of natural aerosols to uncertainty in indirect forcing”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12674).

title: Attribution of the recent planetary-albedo decline
subfield: Radiative forcing, clouds, and climate sensitivity
open: Separate aerosol changes, internal ocean variability, and temperature-driven cloud feedback in declining reflected sunlight. Close attribution against spectral radiation, cloud properties, ocean-temperature patterns, and heat uptake.
status: Goessling and colleagues linked the 2023 temperature surge to exceptionally low albedo, especially reduced low-cloud cover; the cloud-change causes remained unresolved.
why: Distinguishes persistent feedback and forcing changes from transient variability.
key_works: Goessling, Rackow and Jung (2025; online 2024), [“Recent global temperature surge intensified by record-low planetary albedo”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adq7280).

title: Convective self-aggregation in the real tropical atmosphere
open: Determine when spontaneous aggregation in idealized radiative-convective equilibrium controls observed tropical organization. Predict dependence on temperature, rotation, domain size, shear, and surface coupling.
status: Studied since the 1990s; RCEMIP reproduced aggregation across many models in 2020 but exposed substantial disagreement under standardized conditions.
why: Connects mesoscale storms with humidity, radiation, and precipitation extremes.
key_works: Wing et al. (2020), [“Clouds and Convective Self-Aggregation in a Multimodel Ensemble of Radiative-Convective Equilibrium Simulations”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020MS002138).

title: Scale-aware entrainment and detrainment closure
open: Derive cloud–environment exchange laws that work from shallow cumulus through deep convection as resolution changes. Predict dilution and mass-flux profiles without regime-specific retuning.
status: A decades-old problem; large-eddy simulations constrain cases, but organized exchange and turbulent mixing remain difficult to generalize.
why: Improves rainfall, cloud feedback, and tropical circulation together.
key_works: de Rooy et al. (2013), [“Entrainment and detrainment in cumulus convection: an overview”](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.1959).

title: A discriminating theory of the Madden–Julian oscillation
open: Identify mechanisms setting MJO initiation, eastward propagation, scale, and termination. Derive observations that distinguish competing moisture, wave, and ocean-coupling theories, including Maritime Continent passage.
status: Open since discovery in 1971–1972; theories reproduce important features, but the 2020 fifty-year assessment retained major mechanism and prediction questions.
why: Extends useful prediction of tropical rainfall and remote extremes.
key_works: Jiang et al. (2020), [“Fifty Years of Research on the Madden-Julian Oscillation: Recent Progress, Challenges, and Perspectives”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030911).

title: Elimination of the double-ITCZ bias without compensating errors
open: Reproduce tropical Pacific rainfall asymmetry and seasonal migration while removing the spurious southern rainband. Preserve realistic clouds, upwelling, cross-equatorial transport, and energy balance.
status: Identified in coupled models in the 1990s; comparisons through CMIP6 show persistence despite partial improvements.
why: Corrects systematic errors contaminating regional rainfall and ENSO projections.
key_works: Tian and Dong (2020), [“The Double-ITCZ Bias in CMIP3, CMIP5, and CMIP6 Models Based on Annual Mean Precipitation”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020GL087232); Ma et al. (2023), [“The double-ITCZ problem in CMIP6 and the influences of deep convection and model resolution”](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.7980).

title: Forcing-specific hydrological sensitivity
open: Predict global precipitation change per degree of warming while separating rapid atmospheric adjustments from temperature responses. Explain differences among forcings and cloud parameterizations.
status: Energy-budget constraints are established; Pendergrass (2020) documented substantial hydrological-sensitivity variation across CMIP6.
why: Determines water-cycle intensification during warming, mitigation, and aerosol changes.
key_works: Pendergrass (2020), [“The Global-Mean Precipitation Response to CO₂-Induced Warming in CMIP6 Models”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020GL089964).

title: Regional monsoon onset and break changes
open: Predict monsoon onset, withdrawal, and multiweek breaks separately from seasonal totals. Attribute changes to circulation, ocean gradients, land heating, aerosols, and intraseasonal variability.
status: Longstanding; the 2021 monsoon assessment found improved aggregate projections but major regional and process-dependent uncertainty.
why: Timing governs planting, reservoir reliability, and dry-spell exposure.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), [“Monsoons Climate Change Assessment”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-19-0335.1).

title: Forced changes in ENSO diversity and amplitude
open: Quantify warming-driven changes in eastern- versus central-Pacific El Niño, La Niña persistence, amplitude, and transition probabilities. Separate forced change from multidecadal variability.
status: Decades of research; Cai et al. (2021) synthesized increasing evidence for stronger variability in selected models, with quantitative projections still uncertain.
why: Governs connected drought, flood, ecosystem, and agricultural hazards.
key_works: Cai et al. (2021), [“Changing El Niño–Southern Oscillation in a warming climate”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-021-00199-z).

title: Calibrated ENSO prediction across boreal spring
open: Produce reliable event probabilities across the spring predictability barrier while accounting for unpredictable wind bursts and remote influences. Distinguish model error from intrinsic prediction limits.
status: Known for decades; a 2025 NMME analysis found excessive anomaly persistence and forecast confidence behind some false alarms.
why: Enables seasonal decisions without systematically overstated confidence.
key_works: Levine, L’Heureux and Wen (2025), [“Understanding spring forecast El Niño false alarms in the North American Multi-Model Ensemble”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-025-00956-7).

title: Tropical Pacific observed–modeled trend discrepancy
open: Explain discrepancies between observed multidecadal equatorial Pacific temperature-gradient changes and coupled-model responses. Discriminate internal variability, dynamical biases, aerosol forcing, and observational errors.
status: Persistent across model generations; Seager et al. (2022) documented discrepancies extending beyond individual ENSO events.
why: Pacific warming patterns shape global feedback and regional drought.
key_works: Seager, Henderson and Cane (2022), [“Persistent Discrepancies between Observed and Modeled Trends in the Tropical Pacific Ocean”](https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-21-0648.1).

title: Identifiable forced and internal Atlantic multidecadal variability
open: Separate forced Atlantic temperature changes from internal ocean–atmosphere variability without arbitrary detrending. Quantify the predictive information retained in the internal component.
status: Debated for decades; a 2026 rotated-component analysis attributed much Atlantic variability to forcing, with decomposition and model assumptions still consequential.
why: Changes interpretations of decadal predictability and regional rainfall drivers.
key_works: Freveletti et al. (2026), [“Multidecadal SST Variability Assessed as Primarily Forced in the Atlantic and Internal in the Pacific Using Rotated Low-Frequency Component Analysis”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL121516).
aliases: AMV attribution problem; AMO attribution problem.

title: The climate signal-to-noise paradox
open: Explain why some initialized ensembles predict observations better than their apparent predictable signal implies. Identify and correct weak responses, excessive noise, sampling, or ensemble-construction causes.
status: Prominent since 2014; formalized in 2018; a 2024 community reassessment found no conclusive general resolution.
why: Could unlock additional seasonal and decadal forecast skill.
key_works: Scaife and Smith (2018), [“A signal-to-noise paradox in climate science”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-018-0038-4); Weisheimer et al. (2024), [“The Signal-to-Noise Paradox in Climate Forecasts: Revisiting Our Understanding and Identifying Future Priorities”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-24-0019.1).

title: Blocking onset, persistence, and warming response
open: Predict formation and lifetime of blocking highs and their regional warming response. Resolve moist ascent, upstream eddies, stratospheric forcing, and resolution effects.
status: Studied since the mid-twentieth century; 2024 experiments improved understanding of resolution and moist dynamics without eliminating persistent biases.
why: Blocking governs prolonged heatwaves, droughts, cold spells, and stagnation.
key_works: De Luca et al. (2024), [“Enhanced Blocking Frequencies in Very-High Resolution Idealized Climate Model Simulations”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL111016); Wandel et al. (2024), [“Why Moist Dynamic Processes Matter for the Sub-Seasonal Prediction of Atmospheric Blocking Over Europe”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JD039791).

title: Real-world AMOC stability boundary
open: Locate Atlantic overturning stability boundaries under realistic warming, freshwater input, forcing rates, and Southern Ocean coupling. Determine which modeled feedbacks apply to the observed ocean.
status: Multiple equilibria studied since Stommel’s 1961 model; 2024 collapse and 2025 resilience experiments produced contrasting conditional results.
why: Constrains risks to heat transport, rainfall, and regional sea level.
key_works: van Westen, Kliphuis and Dijkstra (2024), [“Physics-based early warning signal shows that AMOC is on tipping course”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adk1189); Baker et al. (2025), [“Continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under climate extremes”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08544-0).

title: Validated AMOC early-warning observations
open: Identify directly observable indicators of declining AMOC resilience and validate their lead times, false-alarm rates, and missed-event rates under imperfect proxies and changing forcing.
status: Model indicators show promise; Ben-Yami et al. (2024) demonstrated major obstacles to robust tipping-time extrapolation from historical data.
why: Converts broad tipping concern into testable monitoring requirements.
key_works: Ben-Yami et al. (2024), [“Uncertainties too large to predict tipping times of major Earth system components from historical data”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adl4841).

title: Finite-record limits of AMOC tipping-risk inference
open: For physically constrained, partially observed stochastic AMOC models under prescribed future forcing, derive tight error lower bounds for estimating transition probability before a stated horizon. Identify observations or assumptions permitting matching upper bounds.
status: Detection-error tradeoffs were quantified in particular models by 2012. The sharper physically constrained bounds proposed here are a formal research target, not an established named conjecture.
why: Separates reducible uncertainty from information limits.
key_works: Boettiger and Hastings (2012), [“Quantifying limits to detection of early warning for critical transitions”](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2012.0125); Ben-Yami et al. (2024), [“Uncertainties too large to predict tipping times of major Earth system components from historical data”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adl4841); Rietkerk et al. (2025), [“Ambiguity of early warning signals for climate tipping points”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-025-02328-8).

title: Antarctic meltwater–abyssal overturning feedback
open: Quantify how Antarctic meltwater changes dense-water formation, bottom-water export, abyssal warming, and subsequent ice-shelf heat exposure. Couple evolving ice and circulation.
status: A 2023 high-resolution projection showed substantial meltwater-driven slowdown; coupled ice–ocean and observational constraints remain incomplete.
why: Determines long-term heat storage and sea-level commitment.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), [“Abyssal ocean overturning slowdown and warming driven by Antarctic meltwater”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05762-w).

title: Global closure of boundary-driven abyssal upwelling
open: Determine how much deep-water upwelling occurs in thin turbulent boundary layers along slopes. Scale local observations to basin transports while closing the energy budget.
status: A 2024 dye experiment directly observed strong diapycnal upwelling in one submarine canyon; global prevalence and parameterization remain open.
why: Connects small-scale mixing to global overturning.
key_works: Wynne-Cattanach et al. (2024), [“Observations of diapycnal upwelling within a sloping submarine canyon”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07411-2).

title: State-dependent Southern Ocean eddy compensation
open: Predict how eddies offset wind-driven overturning changes across climates. Develop closures accounting for topography, buoyancy forcing, and transient adjustment.
status: Decades of eddy-resolving experiments establish partial compensation; its strength and climate dependence remain uncertain.
why: Governs Southern Ocean heat uptake and response to shifting winds.
key_works: Bennetts et al. (2024), [“Closing the Loops on Southern Ocean Dynamics: From the Circumpolar Current to Ice Shelves and From Bottom Mixing to Surface Waves”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022RG000781).

title: Climate effects of submesoscale air–sea coupling
open: Quantify accumulated effects of kilometer-scale ocean fronts on storm heat fluxes, moisture supply, and atmospheric circulation. Validate coarse-model representations across seasons and current systems.
status: A 2025 coupled simulation identified substantial local heating and precipitation responses; their global climate integral remains unresolved.
why: Tests systematic biases from unresolved ocean fronts.
key_works: Vivant et al. (2025), [“Ocean submesoscale fronts induce diabatic heating and convective precipitation within storms”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02002-z).

title: Predictability of abrupt and subsurface marine heatwaves
open: Forecast marine-heatwave onset, depth structure, and termination under rapid atmospheric changes and boundary-current shifts. Establish depth-specific prediction limits and observing requirements.
status: Jacox et al. (2022) demonstrated seasonal surface forecast skill, with strongly varying lead times; subsurface and abrupt-event skill remains less established.
why: Supports advance responses to ocean thermal stress.
key_works: Jacox et al. (2022), [“Global seasonal forecasts of marine heatwaves”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04573-9).

title: Basin-specific marine ice-sheet irreversibility
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Determine which grounding-line retreats become self-sustaining under realistic buttressing, bed geometry, ocean forcing, and local sea-level feedback. Distinguish temporary retreat from committed ridge crossing.
status: Idealized instability is established; the 2025 Antarctic assessment emphasizes unresolved basin-specific thresholds and retreat rates.
why: Separates avoidable ice loss from committed sea-level rise.
key_works: Schoof (2007), [“Ice sheet grounding line dynamics: Steady states, stability, and hysteresis”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2006JF000664); Fricker et al. (2025), [“Antarctica in 2025: Drivers of deep uncertainty in projected ice loss”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt9619).

title: Conditions for self-sustaining marine ice-cliff failure
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Determine when cliff failure can outrun viscous thinning, mélange buttressing, and geometric stabilization. Establish observationally constrained conditions for sustained retreat.
status: Influential since the 2010s; Morlighem et al. (2024) found stabilizing processes can prevent MICI in modeled twenty-first-century settings.
why: Tests a proposed contributor to high-end sea-level projections.
key_works: Morlighem et al. (2024), [“The West Antarctic Ice Sheet may not be vulnerable to marine ice cliff instability during the 21st century”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ado7794).

title: Predictive ice-shelf hydrofracture and collapse
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Predict meltwater-driven shelf fracture, including drainage cascades, inherited damage, refreezing, and stress evolution. Convert vulnerability maps into validated collapse probabilities and timescales.
status: Lai et al. (2020) mapped vulnerability using fracture mechanics; actual failure timing remains unresolved.
why: Shelf collapse can accelerate upstream grounded-ice discharge.
key_works: Lai et al. (2020), [“Vulnerability of Antarctica’s ice shelves to meltwater-driven fracture”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2627-8).

title: Tidal seawater intrusion beneath grounded ice
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Measure heat exchange where tides push seawater beneath grounded ice. Predict resulting melt and retreat while resolving cavities and freshwater drainage.
status: Rignot et al. (2024) observed widespread intrusions beneath Thwaites; converting geometry into validated melt laws remains open.
why: May explain part of observed retreat underestimated by models.
key_works: Rignot et al. (2024), [“Widespread seawater intrusions beneath the grounded ice of Thwaites Glacier, West Antarctica”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2404766121).

title: Transferable basal sliding laws
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Predict sliding as water pressure, roughness, sediment state, and grounding geometry change. Validate beyond the velocity snapshot used to infer friction coefficients.
status: Joughin et al. (2019) improved Pine Island evolution using regularized Coulomb friction; transfer across bed and drainage regimes remains unresolved.
why: Basal friction strongly controls ice-discharge responses.
key_works: Joughin, Smith and Schoof (2019), [“Regularized Coulomb Friction Laws for Ice Sheet Sliding: Application to Pine Island Glacier, Antarctica”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019GL082526).

title: Three-dimensional solid-Earth feedback on Antarctic retreat
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Infer mantle viscosity and lithospheric structure sufficiently to jointly predict unloading, uplift, gravitational changes, water redistribution, and ice retreat.
status: Gomez et al. (2024) showed realistic three-dimensional structure materially changes projected sea levels; that structure remains incompletely observed.
why: Rebound affects both ice stability and regional sea-level fingerprints.
key_works: Gomez et al. (2024), [“The influence of realistic 3D mantle viscosity on Antarctica’s contribution to future global sea levels”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn1470).

title: Greenland overshoot-duration boundary
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Determine combinations of peak warming, overshoot duration, and cooling that commit Greenland to irreversible large ice loss. Include regional forcing and dynamic uncertainty.
status: Bochow et al. (2023) demonstrated strong pathway dependence in two models; no universally measured tipping-temperature boundary follows.
why: Similar final temperatures can imply different long-term sea levels.
key_works: Bochow et al. (2023), [“Overshooting the critical threshold for the Greenland ice sheet”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06503-9).

title: Greenland bare-ice meltwater retention at ice-sheet scale
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Quantify storage and refreezing in porous bare ice across Greenland and its warming response. Integrate with firn and drainage models without double counting.
status: Cooper et al. (2025) identified substantial runoff reduction in southwest Greenland; continental and future-climate transfer remain open.
why: Improves conversion of melting into ocean freshwater and sea-level rise.
key_works: Cooper et al. (2025), [“Greenland ice sheet runoff reduced by meltwater refreezing in bare ice”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62281-0).

title: Evolving debris, cliffs, and ponds on mountain glaciers
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Predict glacier-scale melt as debris thickens while ice cliffs and ponds evolve. Reconcile insulation, localized enhanced melting, and changing geometry.
status: Global models incorporate improved debris and frontal-ablation treatments, but local evolution and parameter transfer remain limiting.
why: Controls glacier survival, seasonal water supply, and hazards.
key_works: Rounce et al. (2023), [“Global glacier change in the 21st century: Every increase in temperature matters”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abo1324).

title: Transferability of the sea-ice deformation lower cutoff
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Determine how the lower cutoff of scale-invariant deformation varies with ice state, forcing, season, and location. Connect continuum closures to floe-resolving descriptions.
status: Uusinoka et al. (2025) observed a candidate cutoff near 100 m in one 10-km-square winter domain, without a comparable summer signature.
why: Governs ice hazards and heat exchange through leads.
key_works: Uusinoka et al. (2025), [“Scale invariance in kilometer-scale sea ice deformation”](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-19-6493-2025).

title: Persistence and reversibility of the Antarctic low-sea-ice state
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Determine whether recent behavior represents a persistent transition, a long-lived forced response, or unusual variability. Identify physical conditions permitting recovery.
status: The question sharpened after 2016; Raphael et al. (2025) found structural statistical change, which alone does not demonstrate irreversible bifurcation.
why: Affects Southern Ocean heat exchange, ecosystems, and projections.
key_works: Raphael et al. (2025), [“A twenty-first century structural change in Antarctica’s sea ice system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02107-5).

title: Calibrated probability of Arctic ice-free conditions
subfield: Ice sheets, glaciers, and sea ice
open: Estimate first-day, first-month, and recurrent-season probabilities below a specified ice-free threshold. Separate scenario effects, structural bias, and weather-driven timing uncertainty.
status: Heuzé and Jahn (2024) demonstrated a wide conditional ensemble range for the first day below one million square kilometers.
why: Distinguishes isolated low-ice events from persistent summer regimes.
key_works: Heuzé and Jahn (2024), [“The first ice-free day in the Arctic Ocean could occur before 2030”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54508-3).

title: Regional dynamical amplification of extreme precipitation
open: Predict where circulation, vertical motion, stability, and precipitation efficiency amplify or suppress thermodynamic rainfall increases. Produce local return-level changes across durations.
status: Pfahl et al. (2017) separated modeled thermodynamic and dynamical contributions; uncertain circulation and unresolved processes still limit regional estimates.
why: Determines design loads for drainage and flood protection.
key_works: Pfahl, O’Gorman and Fischer (2017), [“Understanding the regional pattern of projected future changes in extreme precipitation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate3287).

title: Mesoscale convective-system response to warming
open: Predict changes in organized-storm number, size, propagation, lifetime, and rainfall. Resolve cold pools and low-level jets across alternative climate boundary conditions.
status: Convection-permitting models now represent organization; Wallace et al. (2025) analyzed one framework, leaving broader structural uncertainty.
why: Organized storms dominate important regional floods and water supply.
key_works: Wallace et al. (2025), [“Cause and Characteristics of Changes in Mesoscale Convective Systems within a Convection-Permitting Regional Climate Model”](https://doi.org/10.1175/JCLI-D-24-0251.1).

title: Tail dependence of compound heat and drought
open: Estimate future joint probabilities, duration, and spatial synchronization of heat, precipitation deficits, and soil-moisture depletion. Validate dependence changes beyond observed tails.
status: Multivariate frameworks expanded in the 2010s; sparse extremes and nonstationarity still obstruct high-return-period estimates.
why: Combined hazards can exceed losses estimated separately.
key_works: Zscheischler et al. (2018), [“Future climate risk from compound events”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-018-0156-3).

title: Reliable tropical-cyclone rapid-intensification probabilities
open: Produce calibrated rapid-intensification forecasts across basins and changing climate, resolving inner-core convection, shear, humidity, ocean stratification, and storm-induced cooling.
status: A decades-old challenge; 2025 all-sky assimilation experiments improved prediction while retaining large early-intensity uncertainty.
why: Rapid intensification sharply reduces preparation time.
key_works: Minamide et al. (2025), [“Improving tropical cyclone intensification prediction using high-resolution all-sky Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite data assimilation”](https://doi.org/10.1002/qj.4958).

title: Tropical-cyclone genesis and landfall-frequency response
open: Determine warming-driven changes in genesis, tracks, and damaging landfall frequency. Explain competing thermodynamic, circulation, disturbance-seeding, shear, and ocean-pattern effects.
status: The 2020 assessment found greater confidence in several intensity and rainfall responses than in regional frequencies and tracks.
why: Losses depend on storm location as well as intensity.
key_works: Knutson et al. (2020), [“Tropical Cyclones and Climate Change Assessment: Part II: Projected Response to Anthropogenic Warming”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-18-0194.1).

title: Hail-size and hail-frequency climate attribution
open: Quantify changes in damaging hail after accounting for storm initiation, updrafts, microphysics, and melting. Build homogeneous observations separating climate trends from reporting changes.
status: Raupach et al. (2021) identified competing environmental effects and major observational gaps preventing general regional attribution.
why: Hail threatens crops, buildings, vehicles, and solar installations.
key_works: Raupach et al. (2021), [“The effects of climate change on hailstorms”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-020-00133-9).

title: Definition-robust atmospheric-river change estimates
open: Establish which changes in occurrence, duration, clustering, and landfall survive reasonable detection definitions. Translate definitions into physically interpretable transport and impact statistics.
status: ARTMIP compared over twenty tracking methods in 2019 and found substantial methodological dependence.
why: Prevents event-label choices from dominating flood and water projections.
key_works: Rutz et al. (2019), [“The Atmospheric River Tracking Method Intercomparison Project (ARTMIP): Quantifying Uncertainties in Atmospheric River Climatology”](https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JD030936).

title: State-dependent sensitivity in ancient warm climates
open: Infer changing feedbacks across icehouse and greenhouse climates while separating slow ice, vegetation, geography, and weathering effects from fast-feedback sensitivity.
status: The 2024 PhanDA reconstruction assimilated proxies across 485 million years; feedbacks and forcings remain incompletely separable.
why: Tests climate physics outside the modern observational envelope.
key_works: Judd et al. (2024), [“A 485-million-year history of Earth’s surface temperature”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adk3705).

title: The Holocene temperature conundrum
open: Reconcile reconstructions showing a mid-Holocene thermal maximum and later cooling with different simulated trends. Quantify seasonal sampling, calibration, coverage, and missing-feedback contributions.
status: Named in the 2010s; Kaufman and Broadman (2023) supported a mild thermal maximum while finding additional evidence necessary.
why: Tests reconstruction methods and slow climate feedbacks.
key_works: Kaufman and Broadman (2023), [“Revisiting the Holocene global temperature conundrum”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05536-w).

title: Unique causal explanation of the Mid-Pleistocene Transition
open: Determine why glacial cycles shifted from predominantly 41,000-year to larger, roughly 100,000-year rhythms without comparable orbital-forcing change. Discriminate ice, regolith, ocean, and CO₂ mechanisms.
status: Willeit et al. (2019) reproduced the transition using CO₂ decline and regolith removal, establishing model sufficiency without unique historical causation.
why: Tests nonlinear ice–climate feedbacks and long-term transitions.
key_works: Willeit et al. (2019), [“Mid-Pleistocene transition in glacial cycles explained by declining CO₂ and regolith removal”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aav7337).

title: Causal sequencing of Dansgaard–Oeschger transitions
open: Determine which ocean, sea-ice, and atmospheric changes initiate abrupt glacial warmings. Reconcile ice and marine records while propagating chronology and proxy-response uncertainty.
status: Capron et al. (2021) resolved diverse transition sequences and found no universal ordering across measured ice parameters.
why: Provides stringent tests of abrupt-climate-change mechanisms.
key_works: Capron et al. (2021), [“The anatomy of past abrupt warmings recorded in Greenland ice”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22241-w).

title: Emergent constraints that survive model genealogy
open: Identify observables constraining future responses through physical mechanisms and out-of-family validation. Account for shared ancestry, predictor selection, measurement errors, and new-model failures.
status: Widely developed since the 2000s; Hall et al. (2019) specified credibility tests, but robust general procedures remain open.
why: Narrows projections without mistaking shared errors for physical laws.
key_works: Hall, Cox, Huntingford and Klein (2019), [“Progressing emergent constraints on future climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-019-0436-6).

title: Hybrid climate models outside the training climate
open: Build learned components that remain stable, conserve budgets, and reproduce feedbacks under substantially different forcings. Validate on withheld warm and cold climates.
status: NeuralGCM (2024) demonstrated strong performance and computational savings but reported failure to extrapolate to substantially different future climates.
why: Makes machine-learning acceleration useful for climate projections.
key_works: Kochkov et al. (2024), [“Neural general circulation models for weather and climate”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07744-y).

title: Affordable multidecadal global storm-resolving ensembles
open: Produce coupled kilometer-scale ensembles long enough to estimate forced responses and extremes with closed physical budgets. Proposed moonshot: tenfold lower full-ensemble cost at matched validated skill.
status: ICON-Sapphire (2023) demonstrated integrated kilometer and subkilometer capabilities; sampling, spin-up, storage, and cost remain barriers.
why: Enables direct scenario comparisons of organized storms and eddies.
key_works: Hohenegger et al. (2023), [“ICON-Sapphire: simulating the components of the Earth system and their interactions at kilometer and subkilometer scales”](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-16-779-2023).

title: Absolute radiometric closure of Earth’s energy imbalance
open: Sustain radiation measurements accurate and continuous enough to independently resolve changes in planetary energy imbalance. Close calibration, sampling, and radiance-to-flux errors against heat storage.
status: A decades-old metrology challenge; CLARREO established an SI-traceable approach, while heat inventories provide complementary constraints.
why: Measures whether planetary heat accumulation is accelerating.
key_works: Wielicki et al. (2013), [“Achieving Climate Change Absolute Accuracy in Orbit”](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-12-00149.1).

title: Full-depth, under-ice ocean heat-content closure
open: Observe abyssal, ice-covered, and marginal seas sufficiently to close heat budgets with credible uncertainty. Separate trends from sparse sampling and instrument drift.
status: Argo transformed upper-ocean monitoring; the 2023 Earth heat inventory retained major gaps beyond ordinary float coverage.
why: Constrains energy imbalance, thermal sea-level rise, and climate response.
key_works: von Schuckmann et al. (2023), [“Heat stored in the Earth system 1960–2020: where does the energy go?”](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-15-1675-2023).

title: Attribution of the residual land carbon sink
open: Separate CO₂ fertilization, nutrient deposition, climate, regrowth, and management contributions to regional uptake. Predict withheld fluxes and vegetation-versus-soil storage consistently.
status: A decades-old problem; O’Sullivan et al. (2022) showed globally agreeing models diverge in processes and regional responses.
why: Determines future vegetation and soil uptake of emissions.
key_works: O’Sullivan et al. (2022), [“Process-oriented analysis of dominant sources of uncertainty in the land carbon sink”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32416-8).

title: Nutrient-limited CO₂ fertilization in mature forests
open: Predict how nitrogen and phosphorus constrain conversion of additional photosynthesis into persistent carbon. Test whole-ecosystem allocation across forest types with multiyear manipulations.
status: Jiang et al. (2020) found additional assimilation largely returned through respiration in mature eucalyptus forest; transfer across forests remains unresolved.
why: Resolves a major uncertainty in the future land sink.
key_works: Jiang et al. (2020), [“The fate of carbon in a mature forest under carbon dioxide enrichment”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2128-9).

title: Predicting soil-carbon persistence from mechanisms
open: Predict residence-time distributions from minerals, aggregation, microbial access, redox, and inputs. Validate after warming, drying–rewetting, and land-use changes.
status: Schmidt et al. (2011) established ecosystem control of persistence; transferable mechanistic field prediction remains unresolved.
why: Determines stock vulnerability and durability of added soil storage.
key_works: Schmidt et al. (2011), [“Persistence of soil organic matter as an ecosystem property”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10386).

title: Carbon mineralization after abrupt permafrost thaw
open: Predict carbon fractions and timing released as CO₂, CH₄, or dissolved exports after thermokarst, erosion, and collapse. Resolve drainage, burial, oxygen, and vegetation effects.
status: Turetsky et al. (2020) quantified potentially substantial contributions; spatially resolved carbon fate remains weakly observed.
why: Converts mapped thaw into defensible emissions estimates.
key_works: Turetsky et al. (2020), [“Carbon release through abrupt permafrost thaw”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-019-0526-0).

title: Amazon forest transition thresholds under interacting stresses
open: Determine location-dependent thresholds for persistent forest loss under warming, drying, deforestation, and fire. Distinguish local degradation from self-sustaining regional moisture-recycling transitions.
status: Flores et al. (2024) synthesized candidate thresholds; their ranges do not constitute validated basin-scale transition forecasts.
why: Identifies interventions preserving carbon, biodiversity, and rainfall.
key_works: Flores et al. (2024), [“Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06970-0).

title: Repeated-fire carbon recovery debt
open: Predict when recurrent drought and fire prevent carbon recovery. Quantify effects of seed limitation, grasses, edges, and rainfall changes on recovery-time distributions.
status: Observations establish degraded states; the 2024 Amazon synthesis identifies feedbacks, while forecasts across disturbance sequences remain unresolved.
why: Prevents treating recurrent fires as independent reversible pulses.
key_works: Flores et al. (2024), [“Critical transitions in the Amazon forest system”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06970-0).

title: Old-carbon mobilization through rivers
open: Partition river CO₂ and CH₄ among recent biomass, older soils, peat, and geological carbon. Identify mobilizing perturbations and close land–river–atmosphere budgets without double counting.
status: Dean et al. (2025) provided radiocarbon evidence for substantial old-carbon contributions; lateral accounting remains incomplete.
why: Changes terrestrial-sink attribution and vulnerable-stock estimates.
key_works: Dean et al. (2025), [“Old carbon routed from land to the atmosphere by global river systems”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09023-w).

title: Ocean carbon-sink trends without sampling aliasing
open: Recover regional and decadal flux trends despite changing ship routes, missing winters, and unsampled waters. Validate against independent inventories and autonomous observations.
status: Mayot et al. (2024) reconciled part of a factor-of-two trend discrepancy over 2000–2022; regional sampling limitations remain.
why: Separates real sink changes from observing-system changes.
key_works: Mayot et al. (2024), [“Constraining the trend in the ocean CO₂ sink during 2000–2022”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-52641-7).

title: Biological-pump export versus long-term sequestration
open: Predict how much exported organic carbon reaches century-isolated depths through particles, dissolved transport, and animal migration. Resolve warming-driven remineralization-depth changes.
status: Wang et al. (2023) revised export estimates using hydrographic tracers; regional changes in sequestration efficiency remain open.
why: Surface productivity alone does not establish durable storage.
key_works: Wang et al. (2023), [“Biological carbon pump estimate based on multidecadal hydrographic data”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06772-4).

title: Origin and vulnerability of refractory ocean dissolved carbon
open: Distinguish molecular resistance, dilution below uptake thresholds, and environmental inaccessibility as explanations for persistence. Predict microbial and circulation changes that destabilize this reservoir.
status: The microbial-carbon-pump framework dates to 2010; mechanistic explanation of millennial persistence remains incomplete.
why: Constrains a large reservoir and proposals to expand it.
key_works: Jiao et al. (2010), [“Microbial production of recalcitrant dissolved organic matter: long-term carbon storage in the global ocean”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrmicro2386).
aliases: Microbial carbon pump; marine dissolved-organic-matter persistence problem.

title: Net marine N₂O response to deoxygenation
open: Predict competition between N₂O production near oxygen-deficient waters and consumption in anoxic zones as circulation, nutrients, and microbial pathways change.
status: Tian et al. (2024) reported substantial differences between top-down and bottom-up ocean-source estimates.
why: Constrains an additional ocean–climate feedback.
key_works: Tian et al. (2024), [“Global nitrous oxide budget (1980–2020)”](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-2543-2024).

title: Transferable attribution of methane-growth anomalies
open: Explain successive methane anomalies with consistent fossil, agricultural, wetland, fire, and sink changes. Require agreement across isotopes, transport models, and independent inventories.
status: Renewed growth since 2007 produced competing explanations; Peng et al. (2022) attributed the 2020 anomaly to wetlands and reduced OH removal.
why: Tests whether feedbacks or underestimated human sources offset mitigation.
key_works: Peng et al. (2022), [“Wetland emission and atmospheric sink changes explain methane growth in 2020”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05447-w).

title: Independent measurement of global OH variability
open: Constrain methane-weighted hydroxyl abundance independently of methane observations used to infer emissions. Separate OH variability from tracer-emission and transport uncertainty.
status: A decades-old attribution obstacle; the 2022 analysis of 2020 illustrates material sink effects on inferred source growth.
why: Makes methane verification robust to changing atmospheric cleansing.
key_works: Peng et al. (2022), [“Wetland emission and atmospheric sink changes explain methane growth in 2020”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05447-w).

title: Plant-mediated methane transport in tropical wetlands
open: Predict wetland CH₄ from phenology, species, water levels, production, oxidation, and plant transport. Resolve emission changes independent of inundation or temperature.
status: Helfter et al. (2022) measured phenological control in an Okavango wetland; transferable long-term observations remain insufficient.
why: Improves a poorly constrained natural methane source.
key_works: Helfter et al. (2022), [“Phenology is the dominant control of methane emissions in a tropical non-forested wetland”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27786-4).

title: Warming-induced freshwater methane amplification
open: Predict differing warming responses of methane production, oxidation, and bubbling across freshwater systems. Capture turnover and pressure-triggered events in complete seasonal budgets.
status: Zhu et al. (2020) demonstrated disproportionate experimental warming responses; transfer to changing natural systems remains unresolved.
why: Prevents missing emissions from small, poorly monitored waters.
key_works: Zhu et al. (2020), [“Disproportionate increase in freshwater methane emissions induced by experimental warming”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-020-0824-y).

title: Annual methane budgets for intermittent super-emitters
open: Infer annual methane totals from brief, irregular observations when rare events dominate. Establish duration distributions, detection probabilities, and calibrated uncertainty across operating regimes.
status: Lauvaux et al. (2022) mapped global oil-and-gas ultra-emitters; snapshots do not establish annual intermittent-source totals.
why: Verifies repair benefits between satellite overpasses.
key_works: Lauvaux et al. (2022), [“Global assessment of oil and gas methane ultra-emitters”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj4351).

title: Soil N₂O pathway partitioning during hot moments
open: Partition nitrification, denitrification, and reduction to N₂ during fertilizer pulses, rewetting, and freeze–thaw. Predict brief peaks beyond measured plots.
status: Decades of studies constrain aggregate sources; the 2024 budget retains substantial pathway and extrapolation uncertainty.
why: Identifies interventions reducing total harmful nitrogen loss.
key_works: Tian et al. (2024), [“Global nitrous oxide budget (1980–2020)”](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-2543-2024).

title: Persistent methane inhibition in grazing livestock
open: Deliver durable methane reduction to grazing animals without controlled daily feeding, preserving productivity and health across diets, seasons, and breeds.
status: Hristov et al. (2015) demonstrated persistent 3-nitrooxypropanol effects under controlled feeding; extensive-system delivery remains separate.
why: Extends mitigation beyond frequently fed livestock.
key_works: Hristov et al. (2015), [“An inhibitor persistently decreased enteric methane emission from dairy cows with no negative effect on milk production”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1504124112).

title: Productive hydrogen disposal after rumen methanogenesis inhibition
open: Redirect reducing equivalents into useful fermentation products instead of expelled hydrogen or impaired digestion. Establish stable interventions with whole-animal energy balances.
status: Lopes et al. (2016) documented hydrogen and fermentation responses; efficient recovery of feed-energy benefits remains unresolved.
why: Could improve both emissions and feed conversion.
key_works: Lopes et al. (2016), [“Effect of 3-nitrooxypropanol on methane and hydrogen emissions, methane isotopic signature, and ruminal fermentation in dairy cows”](https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.2015-10832).

title: Rice water management with a complete greenhouse-gas budget
open: Jointly optimize wetting–drying, nitrogen, and residues to preserve yield while reducing CH₄, N₂O, and soil-carbon impacts under real irrigation constraints.
status: Liu et al. (2024) demonstrated management co-benefits; site dependence and coordination requirements prevent universal prescriptions.
why: Transfers successful plot treatments into reliable farm-scale reductions.
key_works: Liu et al. (2024), [“Co-benefits for net carbon emissions and rice yields through improved management of organic nitrogen and water”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-024-00940-z).

title: Whole-profile carbon additionality of reduced tillage
open: Identify conditions producing additional whole-profile carbon after accounting for density, erosion, yields, and other gases. Distinguish redistribution from persistent stock increases.
status: Powlson et al. (2014) showed many apparent benefits reflect depth redistribution; conditional prediction remains open.
why: Prevents overstated removals and identifies effective management.
key_works: Powlson et al. (2014), [“Limited potential of no-till agriculture for climate change mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nclimate2292).

title: Affordable measurement of small soil-carbon changes
open: Detect management effects against heterogeneous background stocks at proportionate cost. Validate hybrid sampling, spectroscopy, and models on independent long-term sites.
status: Smith et al. (2020) outlined integrated verification; expensive sampling and slow detectable change remain central obstacles.
why: Enables credible accounting and small-farm participation.
key_works: Smith et al. (2020), [“How to measure, report and verify soil carbon change to realize the potential of soil carbon sequestration for atmospheric greenhouse gas removal”](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.14815).

title: Biological nitrification inhibition across real agricultural soils
open: Breed crops whose inhibitors suppress harmful nitrification across soil, microbiome, and fertilizer conditions without yield loss. Demonstrate reduced combined N₂O, leaching, and ammonia losses.
status: Subbarao et al. (2021) transferred the trait into wheat; consistent whole-system performance remains unresolved.
why: Provides a crop-encoded route to better nitrogen efficiency.
key_works: Subbarao et al. (2021), [“Enlisting wild grass genes to combat nitrification in wheat farming: A nature-based solution”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106595118).

title: Perennial-grain performance through repeated stress and harvest
open: Maintain competitive multiyear grain yield while controlling accumulated pests, weeds, and nutrient constraints. Verify durable net climate benefits across soils and inputs.
status: Zhang et al. (2023; online 2022) demonstrated perennial-rice productivity; transfer to other grains and environments remains open.
why: Could reduce disturbance and labor while improving resilience.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2023), [“Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-022-00997-3).

title: Crop failure under compound reproductive-stage extremes
open: Predict interacting heat, drought, excess-rainfall, and nutrient effects during flowering and grain filling. Validate beyond historical climates and separate physiological from management adaptation.
status: Jägermeyr et al. (2021) found substantial model-generation shifts in impacts; local compound-event losses remain uncertain.
why: Guides food-security planning and resilient breeding.
key_works: Jägermeyr et al. (2021), [“Climate impacts on global agriculture emerge earlier in new generation of climate and crop models”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43016-021-00400-y).

title: Preventing crop nutrient dilution under elevated CO₂
open: Prevent protein, zinc, iron, and other nutrient declines while maintaining yields under heat and water stress. Validate cultivars across soils and diets.
status: Myers et al. (2014) documented nutrient declines and cultivar variation; broadly effective prevention remains unresolved.
why: Protects nutrition beyond calorie availability.
key_works: Myers et al. (2014), [“Increasing CO₂ threatens human nutrition”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13179).

title: DAC sorbent lifetime under real ambient contaminants
open: Demonstrate sorbents retaining capacity and regeneration efficiency through years of oxygen, humidity, aerosol, and pollutant exposure. Validate accelerated aging against field degradation.
status: Zhou et al. (2024) demonstrated over 100 open-air cycles for COF-999; multiyear commercial lifetime remains unestablished.
why: Replacement costs and embodied emissions can dominate performance.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2024), [“Carbon dioxide capture from open air using covalent organic frameworks”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08080-x).

title: Low-cost DAC measured per net tonne stored
open: Demonstrate sustained durable removal below a declared target, such as US$100 per net tonne, including energy, finance, water, materials, transport, and storage.
status: Keith et al. (2018) supplied an engineering cost basis; Deutz and Bardow (2021) quantified lifecycle burdens. Estimates do not establish continuous delivery costs.
why: Makes large removal commitments financially and physically credible.
key_works: Keith et al. (2018), [“A Process for Capturing CO₂ from the Atmosphere”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2018.05.006); Deutz and Bardow (2021), [“Life-cycle assessment of an industrial direct air capture process based on temperature–vacuum swing adsorption”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-00771-9).

title: Long-life electrochemical direct air capture
open: Achieve useful atmospheric-capture throughput while preventing crossover, oxygen reactions, mediator degradation, and membrane failure. Demonstrate multiyear-equivalent operation with complete energy and materials balances.
status: Liu et al. reported redox-decoupled electrolysis and a 200-hour demonstration on 26 May 2026; scaled durability remains open.
why: Could enable modular electrically regenerated capture.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), [“Redox-decoupled electrolysis for direct air capture of CO₂”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44286-026-00391-2).

title: Field-scale basalt dissolution-rate prediction
open: Predict dissolution of crushed basalt applied to agricultural soils from mineralogy, particle size, acidity, wetting, biology, and passivation. Validate across multiyear sites.
status: Beerling et al. (2024) reported a replicated four-year Corn Belt trial; broader long-duration validation remains necessary.
why: Determines processing requirements and removal timing.
key_works: Beerling et al. (2024), [“Enhanced weathering in the US Corn Belt delivers carbon removal with agronomic benefits”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2319436121).

title: Weathering dissolution-to-removal conversion at watershed scale
open: Measure alkalinity survival through soils, secondary minerals, groundwater, and rivers. Separate acid sources and close watershed balances linking rock dissolution to atmospheric removal.
status: Derry, Maher and Chadwick documented attenuation in natural basaltic watersheds in August 2026; engineered-application losses require validation.
why: Dissolved cations alone cannot certify removal.
key_works: Derry, Maher and Chadwick (2026), [“Critical zone processes limit alkalinity export from natural basaltic systems”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10936-3).

title: Weathering feedstocks with verified long-term agronomic safety
open: Deliver net removal without unacceptable nickel, chromium, or other contaminant accumulation. Determine bioavailability after repeated applications and changing soil chemistry.
status: Trials show site-specific benefits; Beerling et al. (2025) identify long-term environmental evaluation and feedstock variability as scaling challenges.
why: Protects food quality, soils, and downstream ecosystems.
key_works: Beerling et al. (2025), [“Challenges and opportunities in scaling enhanced weathering for carbon dioxide removal”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-025-00713-7).

title: OAE atmospheric uptake before water-mass subduction
open: Verify atmospheric uptake following alkalinity addition before treated water subducts. Quantify location, season, circulation, and re-emergence effects over stated crediting horizons.
status: Zhou et al. (2025) mapped strong modeled geographical variation; independently validated project-scale uptake remains a gap.
why: Added alkalinity is potential capacity until atmospheric uptake occurs.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), [“Mapping the global variation in the efficiency of ocean alkalinity enhancement for carbon dioxide removal”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-024-02179-9).

title: Avoiding runaway carbonate precipitation during OAE
open: Predict dose, dilution, particles, and environmental conditions triggering precipitation. Develop controls preserving alkalinity at operationally useful concentrations and flows.
status: Suitner et al. (2024) measured contrasting stability windows over 20–25 days; transfer across environments remains unresolved.
why: Precipitation can consume added alkalinity and erase removal.
key_works: Suitner et al. (2024), [“Ocean alkalinity enhancement approaches and the predictability of runaway precipitation processes: results of an experimental study to determine critical alkalinity ranges for safe and sustainable application scenarios”](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-21-4587-2024).

title: Ecological limits of repeated ocean alkalinity exposure
open: Determine responses to repeated OAE plumes, separating pH, impurities, nutrients, and carbonate effects. Identify experimental endpoints predicting population outcomes in open ecosystems.
status: Marín-Samper et al. (2024) found no inferred damaging metabolism response within their tested equilibrated range; broader exposures remain unresolved.
why: Defines effective deployment envelopes and monitoring indicators.
key_works: Marín-Samper et al. (2024), [“Assessing the impact of CO₂-equilibrated ocean alkalinity enhancement on microbial metabolic rates in an oligotrophic system”](https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-21-2859-2024).

title: Additional atmospheric removal from cultivated seaweed
open: Measure uptake after accounting for phytoplankton competition, nutrients, calcifying epibionts, and delayed equilibration. Establish additionality against the ecosystem without farming.
status: Bach et al. (2021) quantified possible deductions; published exchanges contest generality. System-specific measured additionality remains open.
why: Distinguishes removal from redistribution of ocean productivity.
key_works: Bach et al. (2021), [“Testing the climate intervention potential of ocean afforestation using the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22837-2).

title: Residence time and ecological consequences of sunk seaweed
open: Determine biomass fate through fragmentation, grazing, decomposition, and circulation. Identify conditions providing century-scale atmospheric isolation without unacceptable oxygen depletion or ecosystem damage.
status: Modeled farming potential and release depth do not establish site-specific permanence or ecological consequences.
why: Determines whether sinking delivers durable removal.
key_works: Bach et al. (2021), [“Testing the climate intervention potential of ocean afforestation using the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22837-2); DeAngelo et al. (2023), [“Economic and biophysical limits to seaweed farming for climate change mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41477-022-01305-9).

title: Biochar permanence across feedstocks and environments
open: Predict biochar decay and effects on native carbon from production and material properties across environments. Validate century-scale retention using observations and defensible aging relationships.
status: Woolf et al. (2010) quantified sustainable potential; Lehmann et al. (2021) synthesized persistent system-dependent durability uncertainties.
why: Enables credible accounting across heterogeneous pyrolysis products.
key_works: Woolf et al. (2010), [“Sustainable biochar to mitigate global climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms1053); Lehmann et al. (2021), [“Biochar in climate change mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8).

title: Engineered wood burial with demonstrable durability
open: Design low-cost burial suppressing decomposition and methane across wood, hydrology, and geology. Detect deteriorating protective conditions before substantial reversal.
status: Zeng et al. (2024) examined a 3,775-year-old preserved log; reproducing that preservation at engineered scale remains empirical.
why: Could store sustainable biomass with little processing energy.
key_works: Zeng et al. (2024), [“3775-year-old wood burial supports ‘wood vaulting’ as a durable carbon removal method”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adm8133).

title: BECCS potential under simultaneous land and water constraints
open: Determine net-removal capacity while preserving environmental flows, groundwater, ecosystems, and food production. Include land-use counterfactuals and supply-chain emissions.
status: Ai et al. (2021) found sustainable irrigation sharply limits unconstrained potential; joint constraints remain scenario dependent.
why: Tests physical availability of pathway-assumed removal.
key_works: Ai et al. (2021), [“Global bioenergy with carbon capture and storage potential is largely constrained by sustainable irrigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-021-00740-4).

title: Full climate benefit of forest restoration
open: Predict time-dependent warming effects combining carbon, albedo, evapotranspiration, clouds, and disturbance. Validate spatial recommendations across forest types.
status: Hasler et al. (2024) mapped carbon–albedo accounting; cloud, hydrological, and disturbance contributions remain uncertain.
why: Identifies restoration delivering actual climate benefits.
key_works: Hasler et al. (2024), [“Accounting for albedo change to identify climate-positive tree cover restoration”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46577-1).

title: Forecasting correlated reversal of restored forest carbon
open: Estimate joint fire, drought, insect, and disease losses across restoration portfolios. Identify mixtures and spatial designs improving retained carbon over decades.
status: Anderegg et al. (2022) mapped US forest risks; correlated disturbances and unfamiliar climates complicate durability forecasting.
why: Geographically dispersed projects can still fail together.
key_works: Anderegg et al. (2022), [“Future climate risks from stress, insects and fire across US forests”](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.14018).

title: Peatland rewetting with controlled methane trajectories
open: Optimize water tables and vegetation to stop peat oxidation while limiting avoidable methane pulses. Maintain wet conditions through drought and quantify recovery trajectories.
status: Günther et al. (2020) showed prompt rewetting can reduce warming despite methane; site-specific optimization remains open.
why: Improves restoration benefits while stopping continuing CO₂ losses.
key_works: Günther et al. (2020), [“Prompt rewetting of drained peatlands reduces climate warming despite methane emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-15499-z).

title: Coastal blue-carbon persistence under wetland migration
open: Predict retention as marshes and mangroves erode, accrete, migrate, or drown. Resolve sediment supply, migration barriers, and eroded-carbon fate.
status: Campbell et al. (2022) mapped global marsh changes; complete future carbon budgets remain difficult.
why: Makes coastal restoration accounting robust to moving shorelines.
key_works: Campbell et al. (2022), [“Global hotspots of salt marsh change and carbon emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05355-z).

title: Basalt mineralization with low freshwater demand
open: Achieve rapid verified mineralization of injected CO₂ using little freshwater or suitable saline water while preserving injectivity across heterogeneous reservoirs.
status: Matter et al. (2016) demonstrated rapid Icelandic mineralization; broader water chemistry and reservoir transfer remain open.
why: Expands durable storage beyond favorable demonstration sites.
key_works: Matter et al. (2016), [“Rapid carbon mineralization for permanent disposal of anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad8132).

title: Physiological heat limits across real populations
open: Determine heat-compensation limits across age, health, exertion, humidity, radiation, airflow, clothing, and duration. Validate population risk without a universal wet-bulb threshold.
status: Vecellio et al. (2022) challenged the 35°C threshold experimentally in young healthy adults; population transfer remains unresolved.
why: Supports realistic habitability and adaptation-limit estimates.
key_works: Vecellio et al. (2022), [“Evaluating the 35°C wet-bulb temperature adaptability threshold for young, healthy subjects (PSU HEAT Project)”](https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00738.2021).

title: Causal limits to adaptation in temperature-related mortality
open: Identify mortality reduction achievable through income, infrastructure, behavior, and public health. Separate protection from migration and composition effects when projecting unprecedented heat.
status: Carleton et al. (2022) incorporated adaptation costs and benefits; causal extrapolation remains uncertain.
why: Determines preventable health damage and required resources.
key_works: Carleton et al. (2022), [“Valuing the Global Mortality Consequences of Climate Change Accounting for Adaptation Costs and Benefits”](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/137/4/2037/6571943).

title: Urban greening that reduces actual unequal heat exposure
open: Determine which planting and green-space interventions reduce personal exposure and illness across income groups. Include humidity, nighttime heat, water, accessibility, and displacement.
status: Li et al. (2024) mapped cooling inequalities; exposure-level and causal health evidence remain less complete.
why: Targets adaptation spending toward actual risk reduction.
key_works: Li et al. (2024), [“Green spaces provide substantial but unequal urban cooling globally”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51355-0).

title: Climate-sensitive mosquito transmission beyond thermal suitability
open: Predict realized transmission while accounting for immunity, vector adaptation, mobility, housing, and control. Validate mechanistic temperature relationships in new climates and locations.
status: Mordecai et al. (2017) linked thermal traits to observed transmission; future case burdens remain conditioned on changing social and biological systems.
why: Converts climate projections into prevention priorities.
key_works: Mordecai et al. (2017), [“Detecting the impact of temperature on transmission of Zika, dengue, and chikungunya using mechanistic models”](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0005568).

title: Chronic wildfire-smoke exposure and protective interventions
open: Estimate long-term effects of repeated smoke seasons, accounting for chemistry, indoor infiltration, avoidance, and concurrent heat. Establish interventions reducing exposure and subsequent disease.
status: Burke et al. (2021) linked changing fire to exposure and identified substantial chronic-dose and intervention uncertainties.
why: Captures health burdens far beyond burned areas.
key_works: Burke et al. (2021), [“The changing risk and burden of wildfire in the United States”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2011048118).

title: Coral adaptation rates that preserve functioning reefs
open: Determine how quickly acclimatization, selection, symbionts, and assisted evolution improve tolerance without impairing reproduction. Test persistence through repeated heatwaves.
status: Lachs et al. (2023) inferred rising tolerance in Palau; sufficient rates across reef systems remain unestablished.
why: Defines where restoration can maintain functioning reefs.
key_works: Lachs et al. (2023), [“Emergent increase in coral thermal tolerance reduces mass bleaching under climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-40601-6).

title: Adaptive management of shifting transboundary fish stocks
open: Design sustainable, politically stable harvest and allocation rules as populations cross jurisdictions. Update biological stock boundaries and agreements before historical allocations fail.
status: Palacios-Abrantes et al. (2022) projected shared-stock shifts; implementable adaptive allocation remains unresolved.
why: Protects fisheries, food supplies, and cooperation.
key_works: Palacios-Abrantes et al. (2022), [“Timing and magnitude of climate-driven range shifts in transboundary fish stocks challenge their management”](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16058).

title: Comparable causal evidence of adaptation effectiveness
open: Build representative evidence measuring reduced losses against counterfactuals, distribution, cost, and duration. Include failures, maladaptation, and performance under later climate change.
status: Berrang-Ford et al. (2021) identified effectiveness, geographical, and temporal gaps in a global evidence stocktake.
why: Guides budgets by demonstrated outcomes.
key_works: Berrang-Ford et al. (2021), [“A systematic global stocktake of evidence on human adaptation to climate change”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-021-01170-y).

title: Durable and equitable outcomes of managed retreat
open: Identify relocation designs preserving housing, livelihoods, networks, and agency while reducing lifetime exposure. Track receiving locations, renters, and excluded households.
status: Mach et al. (2019) analyzed over 40,000 US buyouts; subsequent wellbeing and risk distributions remain less documented.
why: Prevents relocation from transferring risk or hiding losses.
key_works: Mach et al. (2019), [“Managed retreat through voluntary buyouts of flood-prone properties”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aax8995).

title: Aquifer recovery under intensifying climate variability
open: Determine pumping, recharge, allocation, and land-management combinations restoring aquifers while protecting ecosystems and livelihoods. Include changing extremes, subsidence, and water quality.
status: Jasechko et al. (2024) analyzed about 170,000 wells and documented decline and recovery examples; transferable recovery rules remain open.
why: Sustains groundwater as a drought buffer.
key_works: Jasechko et al. (2024), [“Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06879-8).

title: Thirty-year perovskite–silicon tandem reliability
open: Establish designs and accelerated-aging models predicting 30-year outdoor energy yield across climates, including coupled degradation and uncertainty.
status: Open since the 2010s; efficient devices and outdoor trials exist, but the 2024 roadmap retains lifetime qualification as unresolved.
why: Higher efficiency must translate into competitive lifetime electricity.
key_works: Alberi et al. (2024), [“A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017).

title: Manufacturing tandems without a scale-up efficiency penalty
open: Manufacture large modules with reproducible layers, interconnection, current matching, yield, and throughput while retaining small-device efficiency.
status: Laboratory efficiencies establish potential; scalable deposition and manufacturing integration remain gaps in the 2024 roadmap.
why: Converts research-cell performance into affordable modules.
key_works: Alberi et al. (2024), [“A roadmap for tandem photovoltaics”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2024.01.017).

title: Predicting light-induced halide segregation
open: Predict segregation under combined light, bias, strain, and temperature. Design compositions stable throughout module operation and validate predictions on new materials.
status: Recognized since 2014–2015; a 2023 triple-junction demonstration suppressed segregation and reported 420 hours to 80% retention.
why: Segregation undermines wide-bandgap tandem absorbers.
key_works: Wang et al. (2023), [“Suppressed phase segregation for triple-junction perovskite solar cells”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06006-7).

title: Atmospheric replenishment and large wind-farm wakes
open: Predict momentum recovery across interacting farms under stability, fronts, terrain, and offshore transitions. Validate from turbine scale to regional deployment density.
status: Decades of wake research and steering demonstrations provide partial control; atmosphere–plant coupling remains a named grand challenge.
why: Determines regional wind potential, spacing, and revenues.
key_works: Veers et al. (2019), [“Grand challenges in the science of wind energy”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aau2027).

title: Floating-wind fatigue under coupled extremes
open: Co-design platforms, moorings, turbines, and controls for correlated wind, wave, current, and extreme loading. Validate lifetime fatigue across larger machines.
status: Commercial floating turbines operate; the 2023 assessment retains coupled dynamics, scaling, and validated design models as research needs.
why: Reduces overdesign and costly offshore failures.
key_works: Veers et al. (2023), [“Grand challenges in the design, manufacture, and operation of future wind turbine systems”](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-8-1071-2023).

title: Wildlife-aware wind-plant control
open: Detect vulnerable animals early enough to adjust turbines and establish population benefits and energy costs across species, seasons, and visibility conditions.
status: Curtailment, radar, cameras, and acoustics provide partial solutions; environmental co-design is explicit in the 2022 research agenda.
why: Reduces biodiversity harm and project uncertainty.
key_works: Veers et al. (2022), [“Grand Challenges: wind energy research needs for a global energy transition”](https://doi.org/10.5194/wes-7-2491-2022).

title: Decades-long engineered geothermal reservoir productivity
open: Maintain distributed reservoir flow without early thermal breakthrough, excessive water loss, or rapid decline. Predict decades of heat recovery across geologies.
status: Pursued since 1970s hot-dry-rock programs; horizontal drilling and multizone stimulation improve demonstrations, but lifetime reservoir evolution remains uncertain.
why: Establishes financeable firm geothermal output.
key_works: U.S. DOE, [“Subsurface Enhancement and Sustainability”](https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/geothermal/subsurface-enhancement-and-sustainability); DOE (2024), [FORGE multizone-stimulation results](https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/geothermal/forge).

title: Prospective control of geothermal induced seismicity
open: Forecast damaging-earthquake probabilities early enough to adjust injection, including delayed events after shut-in. Validate calibration prospectively at unseen sites.
status: Adaptive traffic-light models and retrospective forecasts provide partial results; transferable prospective control remains unestablished.
why: Protects communities and prevents project-ending seismicity.
key_works: Mignan et al. (2017), [“Induced seismicity closed-form traffic light system for actuarial decision-making during deep fluid injections”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-13585-9).

title: Fifteen-year superhot geothermal wells
open: Develop wells, seals, sensors, and fluid systems operating above 375°C and 22 MPa for at least fifteen years despite cycling and corrosion.
status: Superhot resources have been accessed experimentally; ARPA-E’s 2025 SUPERHOT program targets sustained-production durability.
why: Could increase heat extraction per well substantially.
key_works: ARPA-E (2025), [“SUPERHOT”](https://arpa-e.energy.gov/programs-and-initiatives/view-all-programs/superhot).

title: Repeatable advanced-reactor construction economics
open: Demonstrate standardized projects with predictable schedules and independently documented cost reductions, including financing and site work. Establish when modularization outweighs lost scale economies.
status: Debated for decades; DOE’s 2024 assessment identifies orderbooks, first-project risk, and construction execution as barriers.
why: Makes firm nuclear capacity deliverable within decarbonization timelines.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2024), [“Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Advanced Nuclear—Update”](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/LIFTOFF_DOE_Advanced-Nuclear-Update.pdf).

title: Reactor-specific advanced-fuel qualification
open: Establish defensible fuel-failure and release bounds for actual manufacturing, irradiation, and accident conditions. Determine transfer from specimens to commercial production.
status: Historical TRISO irradiation provides substantial evidence; new commercial TRISO-X campaigns continued in 2025–2026.
why: Application-specific qualification enables reliable reactor deployment.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2026), [“TRISO-X Receives NRC Special Nuclear Material License for Advanced Fuel Fabrication Facility”](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/triso-x-receives-nrc-special-nuclear-material-license-advanced-fuel-fabrication).

title: Closing a fusion plant’s tritium balance
open: Demonstrate fuel-cycle self-sufficiency after breeding, extraction, processing, retention, outages, and losses, including inventories needed for replacement and additional plants.
status: Blanket and extraction concepts exist; the 2021 National Academies assessment identifies integrated closure as outstanding.
