why: Sustains a fusion fleet beyond initial fuel inventories.
key_works: NASEM (2021), [“Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991).

title: Fusion components with power-plant availability
open: Demonstrate components surviving combined neutron damage, heat, corrosion, and cyclic stress with economical replacements. Include remote-maintenance downtime in availability.
status: Decades of tests cover parts of the environment; integrated lifetime qualification remains open.
why: Frequent replacement can erase the value of plasma success.
key_works: NASEM (2021), [“Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25991).

title: Wave-energy control that improves lifetime revenue
open: Jointly optimize geometry, power take-off, moorings, and control for lifetime electricity value while respecting fatigue, storms, maintenance, and failure costs.
status: Energy-maximizing controllers and co-design methods exist; robust economic benefits remain incompletely demonstrated.
why: More captured energy can otherwise cause disproportionate damage.
key_works: Ringwood, Zhan and Faedo (2023), [“Empowering wave energy with control technology: Possibilities and pitfalls”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arcontrol.2023.04.004).

title: Ecological effects of commercial tidal arrays
open: Determine collision, displacement, and food-web effects when turbines scale to arrays. Translate animal responses and flow modification into population outcomes.
status: Single-device monitoring reduced uncertainties; the 2024 OES assessment retains collision and array-scaling gaps.
why: Supports ecosystem protection and evidence-based permitting.
key_works: OES-Environmental (2024), [“State of the Science Report: Environmental Effects of Marine Renewable Energy Development Around the World”](https://tethys.pnnl.gov/publications/state-of-the-science-2024).

title: Stability certificates for current-limited grid-forming inverters
open: Derive checkable network stability guarantees when current limits, saturation, faults, and energy constraints activate. Extend guarantees beyond small perturbations.
status: Droop and small-signal theory provide foundations; the 2020 roadmap identifies unresolved large-disturbance and interaction behavior.
why: Establishes recovery confidence for renewable-dominated networks.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), [“Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters,” NREL/TP-5D00-73476](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy21osti/73476.pdf).

title: Multi-vendor inverter interoperability without proprietary models
open: Specify behavior so independently designed inverters remain stable together and after upgrades. Demonstrate component tests predicting network performance without unrestricted control disclosure.
status: A 2024 experiment with three commercial inverters found problematic regimes despite satisfactory performance elsewhere.
why: Avoids bespoke integration for every device or firmware change.
key_works: Wang, Ganguly and Kroposki (2024), [“Performance Evaluation of Multi-Vendor Grid-Forming Inverters for Grid-Connected Operation Through Hardware Experimentation”](https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87199.pdf).

title: Protection with low inverter fault currents
open: Selectively isolate faults when current limits erase conventional signatures. Establish reliability under changing topology, weak communications, and mixed controls.
status: Differential and traveling-wave methods provide partial solutions; coordinated protection remains a roadmap gap.
why: Prevents faults from causing unnecessary wide-area disconnections.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), [“Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters”](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy21osti/73476.pdf).

title: Black start of large inverter-dominated networks
open: Restore large de-energized networks while coordinating transformer energization, motor starts, load pickup, synchronization, and limited energy under uncertain conditions.
status: Microgrid and hardware demonstrations establish feasibility; 2023–2024 studies identify saturation and overload instability.
why: Ensures recovery from rare system-wide outages.
key_works: Baeckeland and Seo (2023), [“Large-Signal Stability Improvement of Parallel Grid-Forming Inverter-Driven Black Start”](https://www.nlr.gov/docs/fy24osti/87250.pdf).

title: Resource adequacy under unseen renewable droughts
open: Meet reliability targets under joint renewable droughts, heating extremes, hydrological shortages, and equipment failures. Quantify uncertainty beyond historical weather samples.
status: Multi-year studies identify vulnerable regimes; extrapolation to rare compound conditions under changing climate remains unresolved.
why: Annual energy balance does not guarantee continuous supply.
key_works: Sundar et al. (2023), [“Meteorological drivers of resource adequacy failures in current and high renewable Western U.S. power systems”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41875-6).

title: Fast, certified security-constrained AC optimization
open: Solve realistic multiperiod AC dispatch and commitment within operational time limits, with optimality bounds, discrete decisions, uncertainty, and credible contingency guarantees.
status: Open since early optimal-power-flow research; ARPA-E competitions made substantial progress without settling certification at combined realistic scale.
why: Extracts more service from existing clean generation and transmission.
key_works: Aravena et al. (2023), [“Recent Developments in Security-Constrained AC Optimal Power Flow: Overview of Challenge 1 in the ARPA-E Grid Optimization Competition”](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2022.0315).

title: Selective protection of multi-vendor HVDC meshes
open: Coordinate converters, breakers, and protection across multi-vendor HVDC meshes so faults spare healthy corridors. Preserve interoperability through expansion and replacement.
status: Multiterminal systems and breaker demonstrations exist; the 2021 review identifies unresolved coordination and specification requirements.
why: Enables efficient offshore hubs and distant-renewable connections.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), [“Multi-vendor interoperability in HVDC grid protection: State-of-the-art and challenges ahead”](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.12165).

title: Forecast-aware dynamic transmission ratings
open: Operate near weather-dependent thermal limits while bounding sensor error, unobserved hot spans, forecast failure, and rapid wind changes. Validate fallback procedures.
status: Dynamic ratings are deployed and hourly datasets exist; dependable network-wide operational limits remain an engineering challenge.
why: Expands existing-corridor capacity and reduces curtailment.
key_works: Brown et al. (2024), [“Hourly Dynamic Line Ratings for Existing Transmission Across the Contiguous United States”](https://doi.org/10.2172/2476805).

title: Distribution observability with sparse, asynchronous data
open: Estimate three-phase states and topology from sparse sensors, delayed meters, and uncertain equipment while respecting privacy. Produce calibrated operational uncertainty.
status: Decades of foundations exist; the 2023 survey retains sensor, pseudo-measurement, and high-DER challenges.
why: Enables active operation of previously passive networks.
key_works: Yadav et al. (2023), [“Review of Emerging Concepts in Distribution System State Estimation: Opportunities and Challenges”](https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3292793).

title: Dependable dynamic hosting capacity
open: Determine allowable generation and flexible demand with active control and uncertain forecasts. Ensure connections remain safe during communication failures and behavioral changes.
status: Static maps and pilots exist; a 2024 California demonstration assessed coordination without settling general probabilistic guarantees.
why: Expands connections without voltage or thermal violations.
key_works: California Energy Commission (2024), [“Electric Access System Enhancement: Assessment of a Distributed Energy Resource Management System for Enabling Dynamic Hosting Capacity”](https://www.energy.ca.gov/publications/2024/electric-access-system-enhancement-assessment-distributed-energy-resource).

title: Lean-electrolyte lithium-metal cells under practical conditions
open: Combine thin lithium, high-loading cathodes, little liquid electrolyte, tolerable pressure, fast charging, and long life in manufacturable large cells with realistic safety data.
status: Roughly six decades of research; a 2024 industry assessment retains conflicts among lifetime, gas, pressure, and manufacturing.
why: Converts high-energy prototypes into practical batteries.
key_works: He et al. (2024), [“Industry needs for practical lithium-metal battery designs in electric vehicles”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01624-5).

title: Fast charging across battery age and temperature
open: Detect and avoid plating during rapid charging across cold weather, aging, and cell variation without excessive heating or capacity sacrifice.
status: Wang et al. (2022) demonstrated 265 Wh/kg cells reaching 70% charge in eleven minutes for over 2,000 cycles under specified conditions.
why: Enables reliable charging and potentially smaller vehicle batteries.
key_works: Wang et al. (2022), [“Fast charging of energy-dense lithium-ion batteries”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05281-0).

title: Solid-state batteries without burdensome stack pressure
open: Maintain contact and prevent filaments in large cells at pack-compatible pressure. Preserve energy, power, safety, and lifetime including pressure-hardware mass.
status: Conductive electrolytes and promising cells exist; the 2023 assessment retains major interfacial and economic obstacles.
why: Pressure hardware can consume anticipated mass and volume benefits.
key_works: Janek and Zeier (2023), [“Challenges in speeding up solid-state battery development”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-023-01208-9).

title: Cold-climate sodium-ion full cells
open: Retain useful low-temperature charging, energy, lifetime, and safety using scalable materials. Demonstrate pack performance including heating energy.
status: Commercial technology provides a base; the 2024 review retains transport, interface, and diffusion limitations.
why: Diversifies affordable storage for cold regions.
key_works: Bai et al. (2024), [“Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries: Challenges and Progress”](https://doi.org/10.1002/aenm.202303788).

title: Organic flow batteries with economical electrolyte lifetimes
open: Integrate inexpensive molecules, stability, solubility, selective membranes, and regeneration so degradation and replacement costs remain acceptable throughout service.
status: A 2023 comparison of 38 materials found only a limited subset economically promising under its assumptions.
why: Material abundance alone does not ensure lifetime affordability.
key_works: Emmel et al. (2023), [“Benchmarking organic active materials for aqueous redox flow batteries in terms of lifetime and cost”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42450-9).

title: Reproducible solid-state battery benchmarks
open: Establish protocols and datasets predicting cross-laboratory reproducibility while separating materials from pressure, processing, geometry, and reporting effects. Extend to realistic aging.
status: A 2024 round robin supplied common materials to 21 groups and documented substantial variability.
why: Makes progress comparable and reduces wasted development.
key_works: Puls et al. (2024), [“Benchmarking the reproducibility of all-solid-state battery cell performance”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-024-01634-3).

title: Low-cost multiday electricity storage in real duty cycles
open: Demonstrate competitive delivered-electricity cost including losses, low utilization, degradation, sites, and finance. Test the DOE US$0.05/kWh storage-cost ambition on explicitly defined multiday applications.
status: Established and emerging technologies provide partial solutions; the 2020 roadmap’s targets remain application dependent.
why: Covers renewable droughts with less fossil backup.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2020), [“Energy Storage Grand Challenge Roadmap”](https://www.energy.gov/energy-storage-grand-challenge/articles/energy-storage-grand-challenge-roadmap).

title: Compact seasonal thermochemical heat storage
open: Store summer heat until winter with high system energy density, efficient discharge, and durable media. Include reactors, exchangers, moisture management, and repeated seasons.
status: Seasonal water storage is established in suitable settings; IRENA’s 2020 outlook retains compact thermochemical stability and scale-up challenges.
why: Reduces winter electricity peaks and fossil heating.
key_works: IRENA (2020), [“Innovation Outlook: Thermal Energy Storage”](https://www.irena.org/publications/2020/Nov/Innovation-outlook-Thermal-energy-storage).

title: Installed heat-pump performance during cold, humid extremes
open: Predict and improve capacity and efficiency during frosting, defrost, and extreme demand. Validate installed systems including distribution losses and resistive backup.
status: Cold-climate heat pumps are established; field performance, sizing, and costs under difficult conditions remain open integration questions.
why: Determines winter peaks and actual customer bills.
key_works: IEA (2022), [“The Future of Heat Pumps”](https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-heat-pumps).

title: Heat-pump retrofits for multifamily hot-water systems
open: Replace central fossil systems while maintaining hygiene, peak delivery, and manageable electrical demand. Resolve recirculation, storage, space, and high-return-temperature constraints.
status: Products and successful projects exist; the 2024 guide documents application-specific integration gaps.
why: Removes a persistent fossil load in apartment buildings.
key_works: Houssainy et al. (2024), [“Decarbonizing Building Thermal Systems: A How-to Guide for Heat Pump Systems and Beyond”](https://betterbuildingssolutioncenter.energy.gov/sites/default/files/attachments/87812.pdf).

title: Low-GWP refrigerants across difficult applications
open: Achieve low lifecycle climate impact in high-ambient, large-charge, and retrofit systems while meeting flammability, toxicity, pressure, efficiency, and service requirements.
status: Alternatives solve many applications; the 2024 buildings blueprint retains broader availability and deployment as development targets.
why: Prevents refrigerant leakage from eroding electrification gains.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2024), [“Decarbonizing the U.S. Economy by 2050: A National Blueprint for the Buildings Sector”](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/bto-decarbonizing-us-economy-2050-122724.pdf).

title: Efficient humidity removal without overcooling
open: Remove latent heat independently at low energy and equipment cost. Demonstrate durable materials, efficient regeneration, and hygienic operation under realistic ventilation loads.
status: Desiccants and separate sensible–latent prototypes exist; DOE’s 2019–2024 program targets remaining exchanger and integration barriers.
why: Dehumidification can dominate efficient-building cooling demand.
key_works: U.S. DOE/ORNL (2019–2024), [“Separate Sensible and Latent AC System”](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/separate-sensible-and-latent-ac-system).

title: Durable kilowatt-scale elastocaloric refrigeration
open: Deliver kilowatt cooling at useful temperature lift with competitive system efficiency, low noise, and long fatigue life, including pumps, drives, and replacements.
status: Zhou et al. (2025) reported 1,284 W at zero lift over the initial 500,000 cycles; useful-lift integrated lifetime remains open.
why: Could provide cooling without conventional volatile refrigerants.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), [“Achieving kilowatt-scale elastocaloric cooling by a multi-cell architecture”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08549-9).

title: Durable radiative cooling in humid, dirty cities
open: Demonstrate maintainable annual energy savings under clouds, humidity, pollution, soiling, and restricted sky view. Resolve building coupling and winter penalties.
status: Daytime subambient cooling was demonstrated in 2014; durable climate-specific system value remains the open target.
why: Could reduce cooling electricity and improve resilience.
key_works: Raman et al. (2014), [“Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883).

title: Closing the retrofit prediction–performance gap
open: Predict measured savings, indoor conditions, and costs before installation with calibrated uncertainty. Identify installation, model, and behavioral contributions across building stocks.
status: Recognized for decades; the 2018 Weatherization Assistance Program evaluation found major prediction–realization differences in its setting.
why: Improves project selection, finance, and household protection.
key_works: Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram (2018), [“Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program”](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy005).

title: Building controllers that transfer from simulation to deployment
open: Preserve energy and flexibility benefits across unseen buildings, faults, occupants, and weather without lengthy commissioning. Test comfort, safety, and rebound in occupied buildings.
status: Control demonstrations exist; BOPTEST introduced standardized simulation comparison in 2021, while deployment transfer remains unresolved.
why: Makes flexibility from existing equipment practical.
key_works: Blum et al. (2021), [“Building optimization testing framework (BOPTEST) for simulation-based benchmarking of control strategies in buildings”](https://doi.org/10.1080/19401493.2021.1986574).

title: Passive survivability during compound heat waves and blackouts
open: Identify retrofits maintaining health-based exposure limits through multiday heat without electricity. Validate for vulnerable occupants, humidity, nighttime retention, and realistic behavior.
status: Individual passive measures are developed; 2023 compound-event modeling showed major risks and unresolved building-specific protection thresholds.
why: Protects occupants when mechanical cooling fails.
key_works: Stone et al. (2023), [“How Blackouts during Heat Waves Amplify Mortality and Morbidity Risk”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c09588).

title: Affordable cooling access without high-emissions lock-in
open: Provide reliable efficient cooling to underserved households and services with affordable bills. Measure actual access, health protection, rebound, leakage, and lifecycle emissions.
status: UNEP’s 2023 assessment identifies access, efficiency, and refrigerant transition as coupled implementation needs.
why: Expands essential protection while limiting climate impacts.
key_works: UNEP (2023), [“Global Cooling Watch 2023: Keeping it Chill—How to Meet Cooling Demands while Cutting Emissions”](https://www.unep.org/resources/global-cooling-watch-2023).

title: Reliable megawatt charging for truck corridors
open: Serve freight schedules reliably while controlling queues, connector heating, grid demand, and costs. Validate busy multivehicle sites across seasons and vendors.
status: Megawatt Charging System tests provide foundations; corridor-scale service and grid integration remain deployment challenges.
why: Long-haul electrification needs predictable charging during limited breaks.
key_works: Tolbert et al. (2024), [“CharIN Megawatt Charging System: 4th Event Summary Report”](https://doi.org/10.2172/2367301).

title: Auditable end-to-end public charging reliability
open: Define reliability by successful user sessions across vehicles, payments, accessibility, and networks. Build independent datasets measuring usable service.
status: Rempel et al.’s 2022–2024 study tested 657 connectors and documented interoperability, payment, and access failures.
why: Reliable public charging supports users without home charging.
key_works: Rempel et al. (2024), [“Reliability of Open Public Electric Vehicle Direct Current Fast Chargers”](https://doi.org/10.1177/00187208231215242); [arXiv:2203.16372](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16372).

title: Vehicle-to-grid with demonstrated owner compensation
open: Provide dependable services while measuring incremental degradation, preserving mobility, and compensating owners. Validate profitability under real tariffs and heterogeneous use.
status: Pilots and models exist; Sagaria et al. (2025) quantify compensation assumptions, with long-term fleet evidence incomplete.
why: Uses parked vehicles as flexible capacity.
key_works: Sagaria, van der Kam and Boström (2025), [“Vehicle-to-grid impact on battery degradation and estimation of V2G economic compensation”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2024.124546).

title: Reliable partial electrification of freight rail
open: Jointly design battery locomotives, electrified segments, charging, and schedules without diesel backup. Validate payload, lifetime, cost, and reliability under delays and grades.
status: Electric rail is mature; 2024 route simulations support intermittent electrification, while complete operational evidence remains limited.
why: Enables routes where continuous overhead infrastructure is difficult.
key_works: Lu and Allen (2024), [“Intermittent Electrification with Battery Locomotives and the Post-Diesel Future of North American Freight Railroads”](https://doi.org/10.1177/03611981241245996).

title: Mission-qualified high-specific-energy aircraft batteries
open: Satisfy mission energy, takeoff power, reserves, crash safety, thermal control, and economical cycling simultaneously at pack level.
status: NASA reported 500 Wh/kg SABERS demonstrations in 2022; that did not establish a mission-qualified large-aircraft pack.
why: Aviation imposes unusually demanding mass, power, and safety constraints.
key_works: NASA (2022), [“Solid-state Architecture Batteries for Enhanced Rechargeability and Safety (SABERS) for Electric Aircraft”](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220012921); Gould and Fitzgerald (2022), [“NASA’s Solid-State Battery Research Exceeds Initial Goals, Draws Interest”](https://www.nasa.gov/aeronautics/nasas-solid-state-battery-research-exceeds-initial-goals-draws-interest/).

title: Flight-qualified megawatt aircraft circuit protection
open: Qualify lightweight protection for lifetime stresses, DC arc detection, and coordinated fault isolation. Validate high-altitude insulation against service degradation.
status: RTX’s 2025 report met 1.2-kV/1-kA, <100-μs, >99.5%-efficiency, >100-kW/kg and emulated-35,000-ft targets; lifetime and integrated detection remain further work.
why: Protection mass and losses affect electric-propulsion viability.
key_works: Raytheon Technologies Corporation (2025), [“AC and DC Fault Management for Megawatt Electrified Aircraft Electrical Powertrains. Task 1: Circuit Breaker Design, Development, Testing and Evaluation”](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20250005208).

title: Aircraft liquid-hydrogen tank lifetime and integration
open: Qualify lightweight tanks for repeated cryogenic cycles, pressure, sloshing, crashes, and boil-off. Demonstrate viable payload and turnaround in integrated aircraft.
status: Aerospace cryogenic storage is established; DLR’s 2024 work develops representative composite-tank leak and load tests for aircraft duty.
why: Storage must preserve hydrogen aircraft’s potential benefits.
key_works: Koord and Beck (2024), [“Technologie im Test: Leckagesichere Wasserstofftanks dank Bulge-Prüfstand”](https://elib.dlr.de/207579/).

title: Contrail avoidance with verified net climate benefit
open: Execute route changes reducing warming after contrail lifetime, radiation, fuel penalties, forecast errors, and traffic constraints. Verify prospectively across seasons and regions.
status: A 2024 randomized commercial-flight trial demonstrated avoidance with measurable fuel penalties; robust global climate benefit remains open.
why: Offers operational mitigation before fleet replacement.
key_works: Sonabend-W et al. (2024), [“Feasibility test of per-flight contrail avoidance in commercial aviation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44172-024-00329-7).

title: Ammonia engines with low nitrous oxide and ammonia slip
open: Operate efficiently through transient and low-load marine duties while suppressing N₂O, NH₃ slip, and NOₓ. Validate aftertreatment and engine aging.
status: Zhou et al. (2024) improved modeled/design performance using reforming and recirculation; fleet-duty validation remains open.
why: Nitrogen emissions can undermine low-carbon fuel benefits.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2024), [“Ammonia marine engine design for enhanced efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas emissions”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46452-z).

title: Bankable fuel savings from wind-assisted shipping
open: Independently verify annual savings across routes, vessels, weather, and loading. Optimize propulsion and routing including maintenance, stability, deck use, and schedules.
status: Commercial installations demonstrate savings; Lloyd’s Register’s 2024 research retains application-specific integration and evidence gaps.
why: Reduces fuel demand from existing ships.
key_works: Lloyd’s Register (2024), [“Applying wind-assisted propulsion to ships”](https://www.lr.org/en/knowledge/research-reports/2024/applying-wind-assisted-propulsion-to-ships/).

title: Minigrid viability with uncertain productive demand
open: Finance reliable affordable minigrids when demand and income growth are uncertain. Validate appliance finance, tariffs, productive uses, and main-grid-arrival arrangements.
status: Successful systems exist; ESMAP’s 2022 handbook identifies demand, finance, and portfolio scaling barriers.
why: Sustains access after initial grants and commissioning.
key_works: ESMAP/World Bank (2022), [“Mini Grids for Half a Billion People: Market Outlook and Handbook for Decision Makers”](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2022/09/27/solar-mini-grids-could-power-half-a-billion-people-by-2030-if-action-is-taken-now).

title: Sustained displacement of polluting cooking by electricity
open: Meet cuisines, affordability, repairs, and unreliable-grid constraints well enough to displace polluting fuels for years. Measure stove stacking and exposure changes.
status: Appliances establish feasibility; a 2026 agenda identifies persistent technology, behavior, planning, and political-economy gaps.
why: Links decarbonization with household health and time savings.
key_works: Fuso Nerini et al. (2026), [“A research agenda to support the achievement of clean cooking for all”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2026.102382).

title: Heat pumps above 250°C
open: Deliver industrial heat above 250°C with efficient lift, durable compressors, stable fluids, and competitive installed cost across variable loads.
status: Lower-temperature systems are established; Yoo et al. (2025) identify substantial higher-temperature gaps.
why: Electrifies process heat while recovering waste heat.
key_works: Yoo, Estrada-Perez and Choi (2025), [“Investigation of heat pump technologies for high-temperature applications above 250°C”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125384).

title: Retrofitting continuous furnaces above 1,000°C
open: Replace combustion while preserving throughput, atmosphere, product quality, and refractory life under constrained electrical connections.
status: Electric furnaces serve selected processes; DOE’s 2022 roadmap identifies cross-sector retrofit barriers.
why: Avoids waiting for entire industrial sites to be replaced.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2022), [“Industrial Decarbonization Roadmap”](https://www.energy.gov/eere/doe-industrial-decarbonization-roadmap).

title: Flexible electric steam cracking
open: Operate through realistic power variations without excessive coking, fatigue, or selectivity changes. Validate commercial-throughput integration.
status: A 6-MW BASF–SABIC–Linde demonstrator started in 2024; flexible lifetime economics remain open.
why: Removes furnace combustion from major chemical production.
key_works: BASF (2024–2025), [“Climate-smart technologies”](https://www.basf.com/global/en/who-we-are/sustainability/our-contributions-to-enabling-the-green-transformation/climate-protection/climate-smart-technologies).

title: Electrochemical lime without displaced emissions
open: Scale calcium extraction into closed reagent loops producing cement-compatible feedstock with lower total emissions and cost, including electricity and separated-carbon handling.
status: Leão et al. demonstrated ZeroCAL in 2024; regeneration and industrial integration remain development tasks.
why: Addresses limestone process emissions beyond furnace electrification.
key_works: Leão et al. (2024), [“ZeroCAL: Eliminating Carbon Dioxide Emissions from Limestone’s Decomposition to Decarbonize Cement Production”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c03193).

title: Recovering cement paste from heterogeneous demolition waste
open: Recover clean paste from real mixed demolition waste and recycle it into consistent clinker without contaminating steelmaking or excessive separation energy.
status: Dunant et al. demonstrated electric-furnace recycling in 2024; feedstock variability and furnace capacity constrain generalization.
why: Reuses already-decarbonated calcium.
key_works: Dunant, Joseph, Prajapati and Allwood (2024), [“Electric recycling of Portland cement at scale”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07338-8).

title: Low-grade clay variability in LC3 cement
open: Predict and control strength, rheology, calcination, and admixture demand across heterogeneous clays, including poorly characterized low-kaolinite resources.
status: LC3 is demonstrated and deployed; robust use of broader mineral resources remains open.
why: Expands low-clinker binders beyond favorable deposits.
key_works: Scrivener, Martirena, Bishnoi and Maity (2018), [“Calcined clay limestone cements (LC3)”](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2017.08.017).

title: Decades-ahead corrosion prediction for low-clinker concrete
open: Predict reinforcement corrosion under coupled carbonation, chlorides, cracks, and humidity for new binders. Validate accelerated tests against field aging.
status: The 2020 RILEM synthesis documents interacting uncertainties and limited test transferability.
why: Prevents premature replacement from erasing emissions savings.
key_works: von Greve-Dierfeld et al. (2020), [“Understanding the carbonation of concrete with supplementary cementitious materials”](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-020-01558-w).

title: Hydrogen reduction of variable iron ores
open: Predict and suppress sticking, pore closure, and slow final reduction across variable gangue and pellet microstructure.
status: Selected configurations are established; Raabe’s 2023 synthesis documents unresolved kinetics, microstructure, and feedstock coupling.
why: Reduces dependence on premium ores.
key_works: Raabe (2023), [“The Materials Science behind Sustainable Metals and Alloys”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.2c00799).

title: Long-lived molten-oxide iron electrolysis
open: Maintain oxygen-evolving anodes, refractories, efficiency, and product purity during extended operation with commercially realistic oxide feeds.
status: Allanore, Yin and Sadoway demonstrated a chromium-based anode in 2013; lifetime and impurity tolerance remain separate challenges.
why: Replaces carbon reductants with electricity.
key_works: Allanore, Yin and Sadoway (2013), [“A new anode material for oxygen evolution in molten oxide electrolysis”](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12134).

title: Copper and tin removal from steel scrap
open: Remove tramp copper and tin economically enough to produce demanding grades without routine dilution with primary iron.
status: Daehn et al. quantified the copper constraint in 2017; sorting and specialized refining provide partial solutions.
why: Enables repeated high-quality steel recycling.
key_works: Daehn, Serrenho and Allwood (2017), [“How Will Copper Contamination Constrain Future Global Steel Recycling?”](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.7b00997).

title: Durable inert anodes for aluminum
open: Achieve acceptable multiyear corrosion, purity, thermal stability, and replacement costs for oxygen-evolving anodes under industrial bath conditions.
status: Longstanding concepts and demonstrations exist; degradation and operating behavior remain active experimental questions.
why: Eliminates carbon-anode consumption.
key_works: Raabe, Tasan and Olivetti (2019), [“Strategies for improving the sustainability of structural metals”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1702-5).

title: Carbon-free primary silicon reduction
open: Produce silicon without fossil-carbon reduction at competitive purity, energy, throughput, and electrode lifetime, including alternative-reductant emissions.
status: Hoover et al. (2024) identify promising electrochemical and metallothermic routes; direct hydrogen reduction alone is thermodynamically unfavorable.
why: Decarbonizes feedstocks for solar, electronics, and alloys.
key_works: Hoover, Bell and Rippy (2024), [“Emerging Technologies for Decarbonizing Silicon Production”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-024-00913-3).

title: Low-iridium PEM electrolysis with long life
open: Greatly reduce iridium while preserving industrial current density, gas purity, and multiyear stack lifetime under realistic power cycling.
status: Low-loading losses were quantified in 2018; later catalyst advances have not settled the joint lifetime–loading target.
why: Prevents scarce catalyst supply from limiting expansion.
key_works: Bernt, Siebel and Gasteiger (2018), [“Analysis of Voltage Losses in PEM Water Electrolyzers with Low Platinum Group Metal Loadings”](https://doi.org/10.1149/2.0641805jes).

title: Oxidation-resistant pure-water AEM ionomers
open: Make pure-water anion-exchange electrolyzers durable at industrial current density while preserving transport and adhesion without concentrated alkaline circulation.
status: Jin et al. (2026) reported 360 hours at 1 A/cm² and identified oxidative cation degradation.
why: Could reduce both catalyst and balance-of-plant costs.
key_works: Jin et al. (2026), [“Oxidative stability as a guiding principle for durable ionomer cations in pure-water electrolysis”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73209-7).

title: Solid-oxide electrolysis under repeated thermal cycling
open: Couple efficient steam electrolysis to variable supply without excessive delamination, nickel migration, seal failure, or standby heating.
status: Strong steady-operation demonstrations exist; Hauch et al. (2020) identify degradation and scaling challenges.
why: Lowers electrical demand for clean hydrogen.
key_works: Hauch et al. (2020), [“Recent advances in solid oxide cell technology for electrolysis”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aba6118).

title: Affordable delivered clean hydrogen
open: Achieve low delivered cost with verified lifecycle emissions, including electricity, utilization, finance, compression, transport, and storage under stated industrial delivery requirements.
status: IEA’s 2026 review retains cost and infrastructure constraints; competitiveness varies strongly by location and application.
why: Determines feasible switching in fertilizer, iron, and fuels.
key_works: IEA (2026), [“Global Hydrogen Review 2026”](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-hydrogen-review-2026).

title: Hydrogen leakage and atmospheric feedbacks
open: Measure supply-chain leakage and constrain effects on methane lifetime, ozone, and stratospheric water, including uncertain soil uptake.
status: A 2023 multimodel assessment estimated 100-year warming potential near 12 with substantial uncertainty; leakage remains incompletely observed.
why: Establishes net climate benefits of hydrogen substitution.
key_works: Sand et al. (2023), [“A multi-model assessment of the Global Warming Potential of hydrogen”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-023-00857-8).

title: Hydrogen pipeline fracture across microstructures
open: Predict initiation and crack growth in steels and welds under pressure cycles, impurities, and mixed loading sufficiently for pipeline-specific qualification.
status: Robertson et al. (2015) synthesized major mechanistic advances; material-specific lifetime transfer remains difficult.
why: Determines safe reuse versus replacement of infrastructure.
key_works: Robertson et al. (2015), [“Hydrogen Embrittlement Understood”](https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/hydrogen-embrittlement-understood-2/).

title: Hydrogen recovery from porous underground storage
open: Predict recovered purity and volume after repeated cycles involving microbes, minerals, brines, hydrocarbons, and heterogeneous pathways.
status: Conventional gas storage is mature; Heinemann et al. (2021) identify hydrogen-specific processes needing validation.
why: Enables seasonal storage beyond salt caverns.
key_works: Heinemann et al. (2021), [“Enabling large-scale hydrogen storage in porous media—the scientific challenges”](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0EE03536J).

title: Efficient, contamination-proof electrochemical nitrogen fixation
open: Reduce N₂ to ammonia at useful rate, system efficiency, and durability with rigorously closed nitrogen and reagent balances.
status: Andersen et al. (2019) established isotope validation; lithium-mediated advances do not settle full-process competitiveness.
why: Could enable distributed clean fertilizer synthesis.
key_works: Andersen et al. (2019), [“A rigorous electrochemical ammonia synthesis protocol with quantitative isotope measurements”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1260-x).

title: Haber–Bosch flexibility without excessive storage
open: Operate economically through renewable variations while limiting thermal damage, catalyst aging, buffer storage, and restart losses.
status: Conventional synthesis is mature; variable-feed integration remains explicit in the 2020 assessment.
why: Reduces renewable-ammonia infrastructure and cost.
key_works: Smith, Hill and Torrente-Murciano (2020), [“Current and future role of Haber–Bosch ammonia in a carbon-free energy landscape”](https://doi.org/10.1039/C9EE02873K).

title: Low-temperature ammonia cracking with clean hydrogen output
open: Combine rapid decomposition, low precious-metal demand, long life, and residual-ammonia removal at realistic throughput with low total energy loss.
status: Catalysts and membrane reactors provide partial solutions; cracking and purification remain consequential supply-chain penalties.
why: Improves ammonia as a transported hydrogen carrier.
key_works: Smith, Hill and Torrente-Murciano (2020), [“Current and future role of Haber–Bosch ammonia in a carbon-free energy landscape”](https://doi.org/10.1039/C9EE02873K).

title: Carbonate losses in CO₂ electrolysis
open: Avoid or cheaply reverse carbonate formation while retaining selectivity, current density, low voltage, and closed carbon balance.
status: Rabinowitz and Kanan highlighted the penalty in 2020; alternative architectures trade carbon efficiency against other losses.
why: Determines whether electrode results become efficient plants.
key_works: Rabinowitz and Kanan (2020), [“The future of low-temperature carbon dioxide electrolysis depends on solving one basic problem”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19135-8).

title: Multiyear copper-catalyst stability for multicarbon products
open: Suppress reconstruction, dissolution, flooding, and selectivity drift in scaled continuous CO₂-to-ethylene or alcohol electrodes.
status: Kok et al. (2025) identify coupled degradation mechanisms; initial selectivity and short tests do not establish multiyear operation.
why: Enables sustained low-emission chemical production.
key_works: Kok et al. (2025), [“Overcoming copper stability challenges in CO₂ electrolysis”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-025-00815-0).

title: Methanol synthesis with variable clean hydrogen and CO₂
open: Validate fluctuating-hydrogen operation with realistic CO₂ impurities while minimizing aging, buffers, separation energy, and lifecycle emissions.
status: Direct CO₂-to-methanol is demonstrated; Marlin et al. (2018) documented integration, leaving broader flexibility optimization open.
why: Supplies chemicals and fuels using sustainable carbon.
key_works: Marlin, Sarron and Sigurbjörnsson (2018), [“Process Advantages of Direct CO₂ to Methanol Synthesis”](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2018.00446).

title: Methane pyrolysis without dependence on premium carbon markets
open: Continuously separate carbon without fouling and prove low emissions and viable economics when carbon requires durable storage rather than specialty sales.
status: Upham et al. demonstrated molten-metal pyrolysis in 2017; upstream leakage and bulk-carbon handling remain decisive constraints.
why: Tests scalable low-emission hydrogen production.
key_works: Upham et al. (2017), [“Catalytic molten metals for the direct conversion of methane to hydrogen and separable carbon”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29146810/).

title: Capture solvents that survive real industrial exhaust
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Maintain high capture from contaminated variable exhaust while reducing regeneration, replacement, corrosion, and degradation-product emissions.
status: Amine capture is commercial; durable economical formulations remain application dependent.
why: Whole-year performance determines actual avoided emissions.
key_works: Bui et al. (2018), [“Carbon capture and storage (CCS): the way forward”](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7EE02342A).

title: Membrane capture from dilute, wet flue gas
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Combine selectivity and permeance with resistance to water, particulates, oxygen, plasticization, and aging while minimizing vacuum and compression energy.
status: Favorable membrane separations are established; dilute atmospheric-pressure exhaust remains challenging at system scale.
why: Could enable modular capture with fewer consumables.
key_works: Bui et al. (2018), [“Carbon capture and storage (CCS): the way forward”](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7EE02342A).

title: CO₂ pipeline networks with variable impurities
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Validate composition-dependent operating envelopes for corrosion, phase changes, decompression, and fracture as heterogeneous sources join and leave shared networks.
status: Transport is established; DOE’s 2022 review identifies additional scaling and qualification problems.
why: Balances network compatibility, cost, and operating reliability.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2022), [“The Carbon Capture, Transport, and Storage Supply Chain Review”](https://www.energy.gov/hgeo/carbon-capture-transport-and-storage-supply-chain-review-deep-dive-assessment).

title: Basin-scale CO₂ injection without pressure interference
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Predict and manage interacting project pressures while maintaining injectivity and protecting caprock and groundwater. Validate basin forecasts with monitoring.
status: Individual projects operate successfully; Ringrose et al. (2021) identify pressure management as a scaling constraint.
why: Pore volume alone does not establish annual injection capacity.
key_works: Ringrose et al. (2021), [“Storage of Carbon Dioxide in Saline Aquifers: Physicochemical Processes, Key Constraints, and Scale-Up Potential”](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-chembioeng-093020-091447).

title: Detecting small leakage across large storage complexes
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Bound cumulative leakage over heterogeneous storage areas at tolerable cost, with explicit detection probabilities for slow and dispersed releases.
status: Monitoring tracks major plumes; favorable retention modeling does not replace site-specific verification.
why: Makes durable-storage claims auditable at scale.
key_works: Alcalde et al. (2018), [“Estimating geological CO₂ storage security to deliver on climate mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-04423-1).

title: Unknown legacy wells in prospective CO₂ stores
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Locate, characterize, and remediate undocumented wells economically, then predict seal performance under century-scale chemical and mechanical changes.
status: Long recognized; Alcalde et al. (2018) show strong dependence on well populations and management.
why: Expands qualified storage while addressing concentrated leak pathways.
key_works: Alcalde et al. (2018), [“Estimating geological CO₂ storage security to deliver on climate mitigation”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-04423-1).

title: Closed-loop recycling of contaminated mixed plastics
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Recover polymer-quality feedstocks from mixed dyes, fillers, multilayers, and contaminants while preserving carbon yield and reducing lifecycle emissions.
status: Selected polymers can be chemically recycled; mixed-feed selectivity and economical separation remain unresolved.
why: Reduces virgin feedstock requirements.
key_works: García and Robertson (2017), [“Chemical recycling of waste plastics for new materials production”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41570-017-0046).

title: Industrial olefin–paraffin separation without distillation
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Produce polymer-grade ethylene or propylene using durable low-energy membranes or adsorbents under real impurities, cycling, and throughput.
status: Longstanding; Sholl and Lively highlighted the target in 2016. Laboratory selectivity has not settled economical cyclic operation.
why: Cuts recurring petrochemical energy demand.
key_works: Sholl and Lively (2016), [“Seven chemical separations to change the world”](https://doi.org/10.1038/532435a).

title: Low-waste separation of neighboring rare-earth elements
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Separate neighboring lanthanides at high purity and recovery using substantially less solvent, acid, water, and energy on real ores and recycled magnets.
status: Solvent extraction is established; chemical similarity continues to motivate new ligands and architectures.
why: Makes magnet supply less resource intensive.
key_works: Sholl and Lively (2016), [“Seven chemical separations to change the world”](https://doi.org/10.1038/532435a).

title: Low-emission recovery from declining ore grades
subfield: Point-source capture, geological storage, and circular materials
open: Recover transition-critical metals from lower-grade ores without sharply increasing emissions from comminution, water, and waste handling.
status: Norgate and Haque quantified energy drivers in 2010; improvements remain deposit specific.
why: Prevents shifting emissions upstream into mining.
key_works: Norgate and Haque (2010), [“Energy and greenhouse gas impacts of mining and mineral processing operations”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959652609003199).

title: Stratospheric aerosol size and cooling efficiency at scale
open: Predict aerosol growth, coagulation, transport, and lifetime as injection increases. Quantify cooling per unit material across strategies.
status: Volcanic observations constrain mechanisms; the 2021 G6 comparison found substantial aerosol and climate-response uncertainty.
why: Determines whether small perturbations extrapolate to sustained interventions.
key_works: Visioni et al. (2021), [“Identifying the sources of uncertainty in climate model simulations of solar radiation modification with the G6sulfur and G6solar Geoengineering Model Intercomparison Project (GeoMIP) simulations”](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-21-10039-2021).

title: Stratospheric particles with acceptable chemistry
open: Establish heterogeneous chemistry, optical evolution, transport, and environmental effects of sulfate alternatives under realistic aging and contamination.
status: Keith et al. proposed calcite-based ozone protection in 2016; real reaction rates and broader consequences remain unresolved.
why: Tests whether alternative particles reduce side effects.
key_works: Keith et al. (2016), [“Stratospheric solar geoengineering without ozone loss”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615572113).

title: Regional rainfall tradeoffs under solar modification
open: Quantify which temperature, rainfall, and extreme-event objectives can be achieved jointly, and map incompatible objectives across plausible responses and designs.
status: Simulations show global temperature restoration does not restore every regional variable; robust tradeoff boundaries remain uncertain.
why: Makes distributional choices explicit.
key_works: Visioni et al. (2021), [“Identifying the sources of uncertainty in climate model simulations of solar radiation modification with the G6sulfur and G6solar Geoengineering Model Intercomparison Project (GeoMIP) simulations”](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-21-10039-2021); NASEM (2021), [“Reflecting Sunlight”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25762).

title: Marine cloud brightening from plume to regional climate
open: Determine sustained cooling after sea-salt dispersion, cloud adjustment, precipitation changes, and circulation responses, with observationally constrained uncertainty.
status: Perturbations are observed; Feingold et al. (2024) identify unresolved susceptibility, scaling, and regional-response questions.
why: Establishes physical efficacy and geographical consequences.
key_works: Feingold et al. (2024), [“Physical science research needed to evaluate the viability and risks of marine cloud brightening”](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adi8594).

title: The sign of realistic cirrus-seeding effects
open: Determine when added ice nuclei thin cirrus and cool climate versus increasing ice or lifetime and warming climate under observed background conditions.
status: Proposed in 2009; Gasparini and Lohmann (2016) challenged substantial cooling, exposing nucleation and seeding sensitivities.
why: Tests whether the proposed intervention is beneficial.
key_works: Gasparini and Lohmann (2016), [“Why cirrus cloud seeding cannot substantially cool the planet”](https://doi.org/10.1002/2015JD024666).

title: Credible governance of intervention and termination
open: Design legitimate oversight, deployment detection, dispute resolution, and termination-risk management. Test incentives under noncooperation and political turnover.
status: NASEM’s 2021 recommendations advance research governance; no empirically validated international regime resolves the full incentive problem.
why: Provides accountable management beyond physical controllability.
key_works: NASEM (2021), [“Reflecting Sunlight: Recommendations for Solar Geoengineering Research and Research Governance”](https://doi.org/10.17226/25762); Trisos et al. (2018), [“Potentially dangerous consequences for biodiversity of solar geoengineering implementation and termination”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-017-0431-0).

title: Marginal effects of interacting climate policies
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Identify additional reductions caused by individual policies within overlapping packages, including interactions, delayed effects, spillovers, and endogenous adoption.
status: Stechemesser et al. (2024) identify successful combinations; separating component contributions remains harder than detecting aggregate reductions.
why: Directs limited implementation capacity toward additional value.
key_works: Stechemesser et al. (2024), [“Climate policies that achieved major emission reductions: Global evidence from two decades”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adl6547).

title: Transferability of successful policy packages
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Predict which combinations work in new countries and sectors before adoption, accounting for enforcement, institutions, incomes, and infrastructure.
status: Cross-country evidence is growing; the 2024 global study does not establish universal transfer rules.
why: Converts historical catalogs into prospective guidance.
key_works: Stechemesser et al. (2024), [“Climate policies that achieved major emission reductions: Global evidence from two decades”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adl6547).

title: Learning spillovers from green industrial subsidies
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Estimate subsidy-induced future cost reductions through learning and innovation, separating rents, displacement, and investment that would occur anyway.
status: Juhász et al. (2023) synthesize improved identification; technology-specific dynamic spillovers remain difficult to measure.
why: Determines appropriate support scale and duration.
key_works: Juhász, Lane and Rodrik (2023), [“The New Economics of Industrial Policy”](https://doi.org/10.3386/w31538).

title: Durable support for carbon pricing and rebates
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Identify compensation, communication, and institutions maintaining support through price shocks, elections, and unequal household effects.
status: Mildenberger et al. (2022) found limited support gains from studied rebates, challenging simple compensation assumptions.
why: Policies must persist to shape investment.
key_works: Mildenberger et al. (2022), [“Limited impacts of carbon tax rebate programmes on public support for carbon pricing”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-021-01268-3).

title: Bankable demand for low-emission industrial products
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Design procurement and offtake contracts inducing additional production while allocating price risk and limiting baseline payments and excessive rents.
status: Auctions and contracts for difference provide models; OECD/World Bank’s 2024 analysis identifies persistent clean-hydrogen risk-allocation barriers.
why: Viable plants need credible long-term customers.
key_works: OECD/The World Bank (2024), [“Leveraging De-Risking Instruments and International Co-ordination to Catalyse Investment in Clean Hydrogen”](https://doi.org/10.1787/9a377303-en).

title: Place-specific just-transition interventions
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Establish retraining, income, investment, and participation packages sustaining employment and welfare after fossil contraction, including informal workers and immobile households.
status: ILO guidelines date to 2015; long-term place-specific outcome evidence remains an implementation and research need.
why: Reduces concentrated hardship and improves transition durability.
key_works: ILO (2015), [“Guidelines for a just transition towards environmentally sustainable economies and societies for all”](https://www.ilo.org/publications/guidelines-just-transition-towards-environmentally-sustainable-economies).

title: Stable climate clubs under heterogeneous interests
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Prevent free-riding and leakage while accommodating unequal development, trade exposure, bargaining power, and credible enforcement.
status: Nordhaus’s 2015 model demonstrates potential club benefits; stability under richer political conditions remains unresolved.
why: Aligns national incentives with global objectives.
key_works: Nordhaus (2015), [“Climate Clubs: Overcoming Free-Riding in International Climate Policy”](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.15000001).

title: Identifying reducible clean-energy financing costs
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Separate project, currency, sovereign, regulatory, and information risks. Measure interventions reducing costs without simply transferring uncompensated risk.
status: Financing data remain sparse; IEA’s 2025 observatory improves transparency without establishing causal intervention effects.
why: Financing strongly changes identical equipment’s delivered costs.
key_works: IEA and partners (2025), [“Cost of Capital Observatory”](https://www.iea.org/reports/cost-of-capital-observatory).

title: Financing first commercial plants with informative risk sharing
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Structure public support so plants reveal transferable performance and cost information while limiting moral hazard and concealed failure.
status: Grants, guarantees, and revenue support provide partial designs; effects on independently reusable learning need comparative evaluation.
why: Makes demonstrations reduce costs for later plants.
key_works: OECD/The World Bank (2024), [“Leveraging De-Risking Instruments and International Co-ordination to Catalyse Investment in Clean Hydrogen”](https://doi.org/10.1787/9a377303-en).

title: Additional climate finance versus relabeled development finance
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Measure grant-equivalent flows consistently, establish defensible additionality baselines, and distinguish mobilized investment from activity that would occur anyway.
status: Contested since early agreements; Bergsvik et al. (2024) found continued ambiguity in definitions and flows.
why: Makes commitments and financing gaps assessable.
key_works: Bergsvik et al. (2024), [“Is transparency furthering clarity in multilateral climate governance? The case of climate finance”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10784-024-09652-y).

title: Climate-damage tails in the social cost of carbon
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Quantify marginal damages including correlated disasters, persistence, adaptation, nonmarket losses, and poorly observed tails. Make discounting assumptions explicit.
status: Rennert et al. (2022) improve empirical components; uncertain and omitted damage channels remain consequential.
why: Determines estimated benefits of mitigation and resilience.
key_works: Rennert et al. (2022), [“Comprehensive evidence implies a higher social cost of CO₂”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05224-9).

title: Consistent and legitimate national carbon-budget allocation
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Characterize tradeoffs among responsibility, capability, equality, development, and pathway continuity. Design transparent procedures with explicit legitimacy criteria evaluated with affected parties.
status: Li et al. (2025) make warming-contribution assumptions explicit without resolving longstanding normative disagreement.
why: Converts global physical constraints into national responsibilities.
key_works: Li, Pelz, Lamboll, Wang and Rogelj (2025), [“A principle-based framework to determine countries’ fair warming contributions to the Paris Agreement”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56397-6).

title: Causal measurement of mitigation deterrence
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Determine whether removal promises reduce near-term emissions cuts, through which mechanisms, and which policies prevent deterrence while supporting useful removal.
status: McLaren (2020) quantified potential risks; prospective causal evidence remains less developed than scenario estimates.
why: Prevents anticipated cleanup from increasing cumulative warming.
key_works: McLaren (2020), [“Quantifying the potential scale of mitigation deterrence from greenhouse gas removal techniques”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-020-02732-3).

title: Predictive social tipping rather than retrospective narratives
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Identify measurable conditions making norm, institution, investment, or adoption changes self-sustaining. Test interventions prospectively across settings.
status: Otto et al. (2020) identify candidate processes; calibrated thresholds and success probabilities remain unavailable.
why: Could reveal effective ways to accelerate collective change.
key_works: Otto et al. (2020), [“Social tipping dynamics for stabilizing Earth’s climate by 2050”](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1900577117).

title: Fossil phaseout without an extraction race
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Design credible phaseout and compensation leaving resources unextracted while limiting anticipatory extraction, ownership transfers, and disproportionate burdens.
status: Green-paradox theory is longstanding; Semieniuk et al. (2022) clarify ownership exposure without resolving policy incentives.
why: Connects financial restructuring with lower cumulative extraction.
key_works: Semieniuk et al. (2022), [“Stranded fossil-fuel assets translate to major losses for investors in advanced economies”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-022-01356-y).

title: Reconciling product, corporate, and national carbon accounts
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Join process measurements and input–output accounts so territorial, consumption, and corporate inventories reconcile without hidden omissions or double counting.
status: EXIOBASE provides substantial coverage; aggregation, boundaries, and missing primary data prevent exact reconciliation.
why: Enables comparable responsibility and policy-effect estimates.
key_works: Stadler et al. (2018), [“EXIOBASE 3: Developing a Time Series of Detailed Environmentally Extended Multi-Regional Input-Output Tables”](https://doi.org/10.1111/jiec.12715).

title: Independently verified annual facility CO₂ emissions from space
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Infer annual power-plant and industrial-process CO₂ totals despite clouds, sparse overpasses, production variation, neighboring sources, and uncertain winds. Validate against continuous measurements.
status: Nassar et al. demonstrated selected daily estimates in 2017; reliable global annual totals require further progress.
why: Provides independent checks on major emitters.
key_works: Nassar et al. (2017), [“Quantifying CO₂ Emissions From Individual Power Plants From Space”](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017GL074702).

title: Tenfold-cheaper auditable product-footprint data
subfield: Climate policy, finance, institutions, and accountability
open: Proposed benchmark: reduce independently auditable lifecycle-inventory production cost tenfold against a specified manual baseline while preserving coverage, calibrated uncertainty, confidentiality, and reproducibility.
status: Databases such as ecoinvent supply essential infrastructure; this tenfold target is formulated here and has no standardized field record.
why: Makes product-specific procurement and supply-chain decisions affordable.
key_works: Wernet et al. (2016), [“The ecoinvent database version 3 (part I): overview and methodology”](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-016-1087-8).
